§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3.





(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.



[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]

quotes.whole:
Final Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM)
On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science.
EPA is not changing the current:
primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards,
secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and
primary and secondary PM10 standards.
EPA is also revising the Air Quality Index to improve public communications about the risks from PM2.5 exposures and making changes to the monitoring network to enhance protection of air quality in communities overburdened by air pollution.

On February 7, 2024, the EPA promulgated a revised primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS, strengthening the standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM10 (coarse particle) standard at 150 µg/m3; and retained the current suite of secondary PM standards.  On October 2, 2026, EPA provided notice of its intended approach for finalizing designations for the revised 2024 annual PM2.5 NAAQS. View the intended designations for all States and Territories. Once designations are effective, they guide actions that States, territories, Tribes and the EPA must take to improve or preserve air quality in each area.  The EPA will work with the States and Tribes to share the responsibility of reducing fine particle pollution.

§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3.





(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.



[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]

verdict.summary:
CURRENT US NATIONAL PRIMARY AMBIENT AIR QUALITY STANDARDS FOR PM2.5 (primary, health-based; 40 CFR 50.18)

ANSWERS
- Annual primary PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean concentration).
- 24-hour primary PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³ (24-hour average concentration).

1. LEVELS AND FORMS (the form is part of the standard, so both are given)

| Standard | Level | Averaging time | Form / statistic (40 CFR 50.18(b),(c); appendix N) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Primary annual PM2.5 | 9.0 µg/m³ | Annual | 3-year average of the annual arithmetic mean concentrations from a single site, compared to ≤ 9.0 µg/m³ | In effect; set by the 2024 reconsideration (level lowered from 12.0) |
| Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | 35 µg/m³ | 24-hour | 3-year average of the annual 98th-percentile of 24-hour concentrations from a single site, compared to ≤ 35 µg/m³ | In effect; unchanged by the 2024 reconsideration |

Round-off conventions: annual level expressed to one decimal place (9.0 µg/m³); 24-hour level expressed as an integer (35 µg/m³). Both are compared to the appendix N design value, which is rounded before comparison (annual: one decimal; 24-hour: nearest 1 µg/m³).

2. AUTHORITY AND EFFECTIVE DATES
- Codification: 40 CFR Part 50, § 50.18, 'National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5'; measurement methods per appendix L (reference methods) / Part 53 (equivalent methods); design values computed per appendix N.
- 24-hour level of 35 µg/m³ and its 98th-percentile form: carried forward from the 2012 review (78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013) and retained in the 2024 action.
- Annual level of 9.0 µg/m³: set by 'Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter,' final rule signed/promulgated February 7, 2024, Federal Register document 2024-02637, published March 6, 2024 (89 FR 16202). EPA's announcement states: 'EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter... EPA is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards, secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and primary and secondary PM10 standards.'
- Implementation status (context, not part of the level): area designations for the revised 2024 annual standard are still being finalized — EPA gave notice on October 2, 2026 of its intended approach for finalizing initial designations. Designations timing does not change the standard's level.

3. SOURCE CONFLICT AND HOW IT WAS RESOLVED (read this before quoting a number)
Two grounded sources disagree on the annual figure:
- 40 CFR 50.18 as returned by the eCFR 'current' fetch (and a 2016 govinfo CFR snapshot) reads: '...are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration...' with the amendment note '[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]'.
- EPA's PM NAAQS reconsideration page and the 2024 PM2.5 designations page (the latter 'Last updated on October 2, 2026') both state the annual standard was strengthened from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³ on February 7, 2024, with the 24-hour standard retained at 35 µg/m³.
Resolution: the eCFR text returned carries a 2013 amendment note, which is impossible for a codification that incorporates a 2024 amendment; it is therefore a pre-amendment (stale) rendering of § 50.18, not evidence that the 2024 revision was vacated or rescinded. No source in the record shows a later rule restoring 12.0, and EPA's October 2026 page still administers the 9.0 standard. Accordingly, 9.0 µg/m³ is reported as the current annual level, and 12.0 µg/m³ is reported only as the SUPERSEDED pre-2024 level.
One-line verification for any reader: open 40 CFR 50.18 and confirm the amendment note under the section reads the 2024 Federal Register citation (89 FR 16202 / doc. 2024-02637) rather than only '[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]'; and confirm subsection (a)/(b) reads 9.0 µg/m³.

4. VALUES THAT ARE NOT THE ANSWER (to prevent misquotation)
- 12.0 µg/m³ — the annual primary PM2.5 standard from 2012 until the 2024 revision took effect; superseded, NOT current.
- 15.0 µg/m³ — the annual standard in force 2006–2012; historical, NOT current.
- 65 µg/m³ — the original 1997 24-hour PM2.5 standard; historical, NOT current.
- 150 µg/m³ — the primary/secondary 24-hour PM10 standard; a different pollutant, NOT the PM2.5 answer.
- Secondary (welfare-based) PM standards — out of scope of this request, which asks for primary standards only.

5. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS APPLIED
- 'Current' = the standards in force under EPA's most recent final PM NAAQS rulemaking as of the time of the inquiry (November 2026 in the grounded record), not a proposed or future rule.
- Primary (health-based) standards only, as asked; secondary standards, PM10, and other criteria pollutants excluded.
- Units are µg/m³, the standard unit for PM NAAQS; no ppb-equivalent conversion is meaningful or offered for a mass-concentration standard.
- Values taken from EPA's official statements and 40 CFR Part 50 rather than secondary summaries; the stale-CFR discrepancy is disclosed above rather than concealed.

6. ONE-SENTENCE ANSWER
The current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean (3-year average of annual means), and 35 µg/m³, 24-hour average (3-year average of annual 98th percentiles).

Travel restraint system   means a combination of an anchorage, anchorage connector, lanyard (or other means of connection), and body support that an employer uses to eliminate the possibility of an employee going over the edge of a walking-working surface.

quotes.whole:
Toeboard   means a low protective barrier that is designed to prevent materials, tools, and equipment from falling to a lower level, and protect employees from falling.
Travel restraint system   means a combination of an anchorage, anchorage connector, lanyard (or other means of connection), and body support that an employer uses to eliminate the possibility of an employee going over the edge of a walking-working surface.
Tread   means a horizontal member of a stair or stairway, but does not include landings or platforms.
Unprotected sides and edges   mean any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
Walking-working surface   means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
Warning line   means a barrier erected to warn employees that they are approaching an unprotected side or edge, and which designates an area in which work may take place without the use of other means of fall protection.

verdict.summary:
Under federal OSHA general-industry rules, the trigger is 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

Controlling provision: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i). Except as provided elsewhere in § 1910.28 or by other subparts of Part 1910, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by:
(i) guardrail systems;
(ii) safety net systems; or
(iii) personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

Practical statement: if an employee is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge and is 4 feet or more above a lower level, the employer must provide fall protection. Below 4 feet, the general side/edge trigger does not apply, though other provisions may still require protection (for example, certain requirements for dangerous equipment, openings, or specific surfaces).

Scope note: this is the general-industry standard (29 CFR 1910 Subpart D). It is not the construction standard in 29 CFR 1926, which has a different trigger height. Some specific general-industry situations in § 1910.28 carry their own rules — e.g., low-slope roof work is governed by distance from the roof edge rather than a simple 4-foot height trigger, and stairway landings, rope descent systems, and slaughtering facility platforms have their own 4-foot provisions. State-plan states may impose different or additional requirements, so the governing state plan should be checked where applicable.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — VFR RESERVE FUEL, US-REGISTERED HELICOPTER

ANSWER

20 minutes. A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed (Part 91) / normal cruising fuel consumption (Part 135), to fly for at least 20 minutes beyond that point. The reserve is 20 minutes of flight time at normal cruise — not a gallon figure — and it is the same day or night. There is no separate night reserve for helicopters, and no VFR alternate fuel requirement.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT

14 CFR 91.151 (Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions), paragraph (b), rotorcraft:

  "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

14 CFR 135.209 (VFR: Fuel supply), paragraph (b), helicopter:

  "(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

2. WHY THE ANSWER DOES NOT DEPEND ON THE PART 91 / PART 135 QUESTION

The request does not specify the operating rule. It does not need to for this number. Paragraph (b) of each section is helicopter/rotorcraft-specific and both state 20 minutes with no day/night split. Part 91 governs the general operation; Part 135 governs the commercial helicopter operation; either way the regulatory minimum reserve is 20 minutes. The 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures appear only in paragraph (a) of both sections and apply to airplanes — they must not be applied to a helicopter.

3. WHAT THE RESERVE IS AND IS NOT

- It is measured in time at normal cruising speed, not in gallons, pounds, or a percentage of trip fuel. The quantity in gallons is derived (see section 4).
- It is "after that" — i.e., it is additive to the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing. It is not a cushion carved out of the trip fuel.
- It is computed "considering wind and forecast weather conditions," so the trip-fuel leg is a wind-adjusted estimate, but the 20-minute reserve itself is at normal cruising speed (no wind credit is taken to shrink the 20 minutes).
- It applies at the moment the flight begins ("may begin a flight"). Fuel burned before the regulatory "beginning" (taxi) does not count toward the reserve; the reserve must still be aboard at brake release/takeoff.
- No alternate fuel is required for VFR helicopter operations under either part. VFR does not require a filed alternate, so the "first point of intended landing" is the destination and the 20 minutes is not fuel to an alternate.
- The 20 minutes is a floor, not a flight-planning figure. It must be in usable fuel available to the engine(s); fuel in a tank that cannot be fed to the engine does not satisfy it.
- The pilot in command remains separately obligated by 14 CFR 91.103 to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including known traffic delays and forecast conditions, and by 91.167/135.223 if any portion is conducted IFR. Those obligations can require more than 20 minutes; they cannot require less.

4. CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A QUANTITY (PROCEDURE)

Step 1. Establish normal cruising speed and the corresponding fuel consumption (gal/hr or lb/hr) from the Rotorcraft Flight Manual cruise data for the planned cruise power setting and altitude.
Step 2. Reserve quantity = cruise fuel flow x (20 / 60) = cruise fuel flow / 3.
Step 3. Add to the wind-adjusted trip fuel to the first point of intended landing.
Step 4. Compare the sum to usable fuel aboard at takeoff (not total tank capacity; not including unusable fuel). If the sum exceeds usable fuel, the flight cannot legally begin.

Worked examples (arithmetic shown so it can be checked):
- 300 lb/hr at normal cruise: 300 x 20/60 = 100 lb reserve. At 6.7 lb/gal Jet A that is about 14.9 gal.
- 20 gal/hr at normal cruise: 20 x 20/60 = 6.67 gal reserve.
- 180 lb/hr at normal cruise: 180 / 3 = 60 lb reserve.

5. VERIFICATION IN PRACTICE

- Compute the reserve from the RFM cruise chart, not from a gauge reading alone, and record it on the load/fuel sheet (trip fuel + 20-minute reserve = minimum fuel at takeoff).
- Confirm usable fuel aboard by gauge, dipstick, or fuel-load record per the aircraft's equipment; the aircraft must have a operable fuel gauge indicating quantity for each tank under 14 CFR 91.205 where that equipment list applies.
- Post-flight, any landing with less than the planned 20-minute equivalent indicates the planning basis was wrong and should be corrected before the next flight.

6. SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER

- Applies to US-registered civil helicopters operating under FAA rules (Part 91 or Part 135), day or night, VFR.
- Does not cover Part 121, military, or foreign-registry operations.
- Does not address IFR fuel planning (91.167 / 135.223), VFR over-the-top passenger operations (135.211), or powered-lift aircraft, which are governed by other provisions.
- Operator, insurer, or company fuel policies may impose a larger reserve than 20 minutes; such policies are additive to, and never a substitute for, the regulatory minimum stated here.

CITATION BASIS: 14 CFR 91.151(b) and 14 CFR 135.209(b), as published in the eCFR and the 2026 CFR bound volumes; FAA guidance material (FAA media 32056) item 15 confirms that for Part 135 helicopter VFR operations the required reserve is 20 minutes both day and night, with alternate fuel not applicable.

Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.

quotes.whole:
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo
This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.¶

Acknowledgements
Authors' Addresses
1.  Introduction
Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1
[RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now
itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446].  Datagram Transport
Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS
1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate
TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.  Accordingly, the aforementioned
documents have been moved to Historic status.
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:
*  They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.
*  There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites,
especially authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD)
ciphers, which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2.  Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in
the registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447],
which indicates that such entries are not recommended by the IETF.
*  The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is **RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021; part of BCP 195, which is the current best-practice guidance for TLS usage formerly anchored in RFC 7525).

2. It gave the RFCs that had defined those versions — **RFC 2246** (TLS 1.0, January 1999) and **RFC 4346** (TLS 1.1, April 2006) — the status **Historic**.

SOURCES AND EXACT WORDING

- RFC 8996, Abstract (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html): "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."
- RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction): "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008 ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 2246 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2246/): status field reads "Historic" (the document's own 1999 header read "Category: Standards Track").
- RFC Editor info page for RFC 4346 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4346/): status field reads "Historic" (the document's own 2006 header read "Category: Standards Track").
- IETF Datatracker history (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/): RFC 8996 published 2021-03-23; the RFC Editor sync record carries the same abstract text quoted above.

HOW THE STATUS WAS EXPRESSED (precision points a reader may need)

- The action is a **document status change to Historic**, not an "Obsoletes: 2246, 4346" header line. The distinction matters: both documents were already *obsolete* in the supersession sense before RFC 8996 — RFC 2246 was obsoleted by RFC 4346, and RFC 4346 was obsoleted by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2, 2008). "Obsolete" (superseded by a newer specification) and "Historic" (no longer recommended for new use; retired from the standards track) are different axes, and RFC 8996's contribution is the second one. The RFC Editor info pages show both facts side by side: "Historic" in the status field, plus "This RFC is now obsolete, see RFC 4346" / "see RFC 5246" as separate notes.
- RFC 8996 itself is **not** Standards Track; its "Status of This Memo" reads "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice." It is therefore the BCP-track document that retires the two Standards Track specifications.
- Scope note: the same document also deprecates **DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347)** — note 4347, not 4346 — and moves it to Historic, but explicitly does *not* deprecate DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347), and observes there is no DTLS 1.1. It additionally moves RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) to Historic and updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1.

MINIMAL CITATION FORM

  RFC 8996 ("Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", March 2021, BCP 195) deprecates TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) and moves both to Historic status.

Español

Contribution and Benefit Base Determination
Automatic Determinations
Contribution & Benefit Base
Wage-indexed Amounts
Method for determining the base
The formula for determining the OASDI contribution and benefit base
is set by law. The formula is applicable only if a
cost-of-living increase becomes
effective for December of the year in which a determination of
the base would ordinarily be made.  Because there is a cost-of-living increase for December 2026, the
formula is applicable.  The formula states that the base for any year
Y after 1994 is equal to the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by
the ratio of the national average wage index for
year (Y-2) to that for 1992, with the result rounded to the nearest
multiple of $300.  If the result is less than the current base, the base
is not reduced.
Base for 2027
Under the above formula, the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600
multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for
1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500.  If the amount so determined
is not a multiple of $300, it is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar/tax year 2026 is $184,500.

DEFINITION AND SCOPE

- The contribution and benefit base is the annual limit on earnings subject to Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) taxation; the same limit applies when those earnings are used in a benefit computation. SSA calls it the 'taxable maximum' (SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html).
- It applies to wages for employees and to self-employment income. The OASDI rate is 6.2% each for employee and employer (12.4% for the self-employed).
- It does NOT apply to Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI): there has been no HI taxable maximum since 1994, and the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax (individual earned income over $200,000 / $250,000 MFJ) sits outside this cap.

SOURCE CONFIRMATION (three independent SSA publications, all agreeing)

1. SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet, '2026 SOCIAL SECURITY CHANGES', Maximum Taxable Earnings table (https://www.ssa.gov/cola/factsheets/2026.html):
   'Maximum Taxable Earnings — Social Security (OASDI only): 2025 $176,100 | 2026 $184,500. Medicare (HI only): No Limit.'
2. SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 specifications (https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf):
   'The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500. The employer and employee tax rate for Social Security will be withheld at 6.2 percent (up to $11,439.00).' The record layout repeats the limit: 'should not exceed the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026)' and 'should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026.'
3. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Contribution and Benefit Base table (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html): 2025 $176,100; 2026 $184,500; 2027 $192,300.

Because the OACT table now also carries 2027 ($192,300), the 2026 figure of $184,500 is final and no longer subject to revision. The 2027 figure is NOT the answer to this question and is cited only as confirmation.

ARITHMETIC CHECKS (all consistent with the $184,500 base)

- Maximum employee OASDI tax: 184,500 x 0.062 = $11,439.00 (matches the EFW2 stated cap exactly).
- Maximum employer OASDI tax: $11,439.00 (same).
- Combined employee + employer maximum: 184,500 x 0.124 = $22,878.00.
- Maximum self-employment OASDI tax: 184,500 x 0.124 = $22,878.00.
- Year-over-year change: 184,500 - 176,100 = $8,400, i.e. 8,400 / 176,100 = 4.77% increase over 2025.
- Medicare: uncapped, so no maximum HI tax (employee 1.45% on all wages, plus 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above the thresholds).

STATUTORY MECHANISM

Under the automatic-adjustment formula, the base for a year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y-2) to that for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The 2026 base is a multiple of $300 (184,500 / 300 = 615), as required. (The OACT 'determination' pages currently posted describe the 2027 determination — $60,600 x 72,800.33 / 22,935.42 = $192,353.14, rounding to $192,300 — which illustrates the same formula and is consistent with the 2026 base of $184,500 being the floor it had to exceed.)

CORRECTION TO A STATED ASSUMPTION

The project context assumed that 2025 legislation 'introduced a new additional taxable earnings tier above the traditional base' so that 2026 must be reported under a 'two-tier structure.' None of the authoritative SSA sources above shows any such tier for 2026: the COLA fact sheet, the EFW2 TY2026 specifications, and the OACT base table all describe a single OASDI taxable maximum of $184,500 with a single 6.2%/12.4% rate. The answer is therefore reported on the single-tier basis; the two-tier premise is unsupported by the grounding and should not be carried into downstream work.

RELATED 2026 FIGURES (context only; often confused with the base)

- Quarter of Coverage: $1,890 (2025: $1,810).
- Retirement Earnings Test exempt amounts: $24,480/yr ($2,040/mo) under FRA; $65,160/yr ($5,430/mo) in the year FRA is reached.
- SGA: $1,690/mo non-blind; $2,830/mo blind. TWP: $1,210/mo.
- COLA for 2026: 2.8%. Combined employee/self-employed FICA rate: 7.65% / 15.30% (Social Security plus Medicare).
- Old-law contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100 (used for Railroad Retirement tier II, PBGC guarantees, and special-minimum year-of-coverage determinations) — a different quantity from the $184,500 current-law base and not a substitute for it.

BOTTOM LINE FOR A PAYROLL OR TAX IMPLEMENTATION

Cap OASDI-taxable wages and self-employment income at $184,500 for tax year 2026; withhold/accrue at most $11,439.00 of employee Social Security tax and $11,439.00 of employer Social Security tax per employee (combined $22,878.00); apply Medicare HI with no cap. Do not use the 2025 figure of $176,100 or the 2027 figure of $192,300 for 2026.

The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less. The elective deferral limit for SIMPLE plans is 100% of compensation or $17,000 in 2026, $16,500 in 2025, $16,000 in 2024, and $15,500 in 2023. Time for depositing elective deferrals
Employers must deposit employee contributions to the retirement plan's trust or individual accounts as soon as they can reasonably be segregated from the employer's general assets. The Department of Labor provides a 7-business-day safe harbor rule for employee contributions to plans with fewer than 100 participants.

Employer matching contributions. If the plan document permits, the employer can make matching contributions for an employee who contributes elective deferrals (for example, 50 cents for each dollar deferred). verdict.summary:
ANSWER

For the 2026 tax year, the limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan — before any catch-up contribution — is $24,500.

Equivalently: $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less. Because the compensation prong only binds at very low pay levels (an employee earning under $24,500 for the year), the practical answer for essentially every participant is the flat dollar figure of $24,500.

1. AUTHORITY AND SOURCING

- Governing rule: IRC §402(g)(1), the annual limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in §402(g)(3), as adjusted for inflation and published in the IRS's annual cost-of-living notice.
- Controlling 2026 figure: IRS Notice 2025-67. The notice states: 'The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.'
- Corroborating IRS publications for 2026, all consistent:
  * Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: 'The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
  * Retirement Topics — Contributions: 'The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.'
  * Publication 560: 'The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026.'
  * Publication 571: 'Therefore, the limit on elective deferrals for 2026 is $24,500.'
- Status of the figure: Notice 2025-67 is the IRS's published annual COLA notice; the 2026 figure is final for the year, not a draft or proposal. (Statutory indexing means later legislation could change it, but no such change is reflected in the sources consulted.)

2. WHAT COUNTS TOWARD THE $24,500

- Pre-tax (traditional) elective deferrals and designated Roth elective deferrals count toward the same single $24,500 limit. A participant cannot defer $24,500 pre-tax and another $24,500 as Roth; the two are aggregated.
- The limit is per individual, per calendar year, and applies across all plans of the same type in which the individual participates — the IRS instructs: 'Generally, you aggregate all elective deferrals you made to all plans in which you participate to determine if you have exceeded these limits.' The same $24,500 ceiling is shared with 403(b) plans, SARSEPs, and (for the basic limit context) other §402(g)-type arrangements; a SIMPLE plan has its own lower figure.
- Employer matching and employer nonelective contributions do not count against the $24,500; they count against the separate annual additions limit.
- After-tax (non-Roth) employee contributions do not count against the $24,500; they are limited by §415 and §401(m).

3. WHAT IS EXCLUDED FROM THE $24,500 (the catch-up layer, for completeness)

These are additive to, not part of, the requested figure:
- Age 50+ catch-up (2026): $8,000, up from $7,500 (Notice 2025-67; §414(v)(2)(B)(i)). Available only if the plan permits.
- Age 60–63 enhanced catch-up (2026): $11,250, unchanged (Notice 2025-67; §414(v)(2)(E)(i)). This replaces, rather than stacks on top of, the $8,000 for those attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026.
- SIMPLE 401(k) and SIMPLE IRA catch-up (2026): $4,000 generally; $5,250 for ages 60–63; $3,850 for certain SIMPLE plans.
So a 2026 participant aged 50–59 who is plan-eligible for catch-up could defer up to $32,500 ($24,500 + $8,000); one aged 60–63 could defer up to $35,750 ($24,500 + $11,250). Neither of those is the answer to this question.

4. ADJACENT 2026 LIMITS — FOR DISAMBIGUATION ONLY (do not confuse with the answer)

- §415(c) annual additions limit (all sources, employee + employer, excluding catch-up): $72,000 (up from $70,000). The $24,500 deferral limit sits well inside this; $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500 is also inside it.
- §401(a)(17) compensation limit: $360,000 (up from $350,000).
- SIMPLE 401(k)/SIMPLE IRA salary reduction limit: $17,000 (up from $16,500); $18,100 for certain SIMPLE plans under SECURE 2.0 §117.
- §457(e)(15) state/local government and tax-exempt deferred compensation limit: $24,500 (same as the 401(k) figure, per Notice 2025-67).
- IRA contribution limit: $7,500, plus $1,100 age-50 catch-up.

5. PLAN-LEVEL AND TESTING CONSTRAINTS THAT CAN REDUCE AN INDIVIDUAL'S EFFECTIVE DEFERRAL BELOW $24,500

$24,500 is a statutory ceiling, not an entitlement. HR/payroll should communicate it as a maximum, because:
- Plan terms may impose a lower cap (for example, a 15% of pay deferral cap, or a per-paycheck percentage cap).
- ADP nondiscrimination testing under §401(k)(3) can force refunds or in-plan recharacterization of excess contributions for highly compensated employees, effectively lowering the amount an HCE may keep for the year. The IRS states plainly: 'If you are a manager, owner, or highly compensated employee, your plan might need to limit your deferrals to pass nondiscrimination tests.'
- A participant's own compensation can bind the limit if compensation for the year is below $24,500.
- In a 403(b) plan, the separate 15-years-of-service catch-up and the elective deferral limit interaction can change the operative number; that does not apply to a 401(k).

6. OPERATIONAL PROCEDURE (HR / payroll / plan administration)

Step 1 — Set the system limit. Configure the payroll deferral engine with a 2026 calendar-year employee-deferral cap of $24,500 per participant, applied to the sum of pre-tax plus Roth elective deferrals, and tracked per individual across all plans of the employer that share the §402(g) limit (including any 403(b) or SARSEP arrangement, and excluding SIMPLE deferrals, which use $17,000).

Step 2 — Set catch-up as a separate, additive bucket. If the plan permits catch-up, configure $8,000 for participants who attain age 50 or older by 12/31/2026, and $11,250 for those who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 during 2026 — with the $11,250 replacing the $8,000 rather than adding to it. Do not let catch-up amounts consume the $24,500 bucket, and do not let them count against the $72,000 annual additions limit.

Step 3 — Per-paycheck pacing. Compute the per-pay-period maximum as $24,500 divided by the number of remaining pay periods, and stop deferrals when the cumulative year-to-date employee elective deferral total reaches $24,500 (plus any permitted catch-up). Watch for front-loading: a participant deferring 100% of pay can hit the cap mid-year, and the plan must then suspend deferrals or spill into catch-up if eligible.

Step 4 — Multi-employer / mid-year hires. Obtain prior-employer deferral totals from the participant (the plan may rely on the participant's certification) and reduce the remaining allowable deferral accordingly, because the $24,500 limit is per person, not per plan. For a mid-year hire with no prior deferrals, the full $24,500 remains available.

Step 5 — Excess deferral correction. If employee elective deferrals exceed $24,500 for 2026 (excluding valid catch-up), the excess is includible in the employee's gross income. The participant must generally notify the plan and request a corrective distribution of the excess (adjusted for earnings) by April 15, 2027 to avoid double taxation; if the excess arose in one plan, the plan may distribute it under the EPCRS Self-Correction Program (Appendix A §.04 addresses failure to distribute §402(g) excesses). Coordinate with the recordkeeper and issue a corrected Form 1099-R / W-2 as required.

Step 6 — Communications. In open-enrollment and payroll notices, state: 'The 2026 IRS limit on your elective deferrals is $24,500. If you are 50 or older, you may defer an additional $8,000 (or $11,250 if you turn 60–63 in 2026) if the plan permits catch-up contributions. Your plan may impose a lower limit, and highly compensated employees may be subject to further limits under nondiscrimination testing.'

7. SCOPE AND ASSUMPTIONS

- Jurisdiction: United States. '401(k) plan' is a US-specific plan type governed by the IRC; the authority is the IRS.
- The figure is the base §402(g) elective deferral limit, i.e., excluding catch-up contributions, as the question specifies.
- The figure is stated for a non-SIMPLE 401(k). A SIMPLE 401(k) uses $17,000 for 2026.
- The figure is a dollar cap per individual per calendar year, subject to the lesser-of-100%-of-compensation rule.

8. CONSISTENCY CHECK

$24,500 < $72,000 (§415(c) annual additions) ✓. $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500 < $72,000 ✓. $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750 < $72,000 ✓. $24,500 < $360,000 (§401(a)(17) compensation cap) ✓. $24,500 > $17,000 (SIMPLE 401(k)) ✓, consistent with SIMPLE being a carve-out. All stated 2026 figures match Notice 2025-67 and the IRS topic pages and publications cited.

quotes.whole:
§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3.





(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.



[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]

(132.6 KB)
On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science.
EPA is not changing the current:
primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards,
secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and
primary and secondary PM10 standards.
EPA is also revising the Air Quality Index to improve public communications about the risks from PM2.5 exposures and making changes to the monitoring network to enhance protection of air quality in communities overburdened by air pollution.

Air Monitoring for Fine Particle Pollution (PM2.5)
Fact Sheet
Summary
• On February 7, 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) strengthened the
National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for fine particle pollution (PM2.5) by
revising the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard to 9.0 micrograms
per cubic meter (µg/m3). EPA is retaining the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard, with its
level of 35 µg/m3.

provides public health protection against exposures to coarse particles. The
Administrator concludes that current evidence does not call into question the adequacy
of that standard.

both PM2.5 and PM10 at this time. The Administrator concludes that the available
evidence and information do not call into question the adequacy of protection provided
by the current secondary PM standards for non-ecological effects (i.e., visibility, climate,
and materials effects).

communities in reducing exposures and will also help inform future PM NAAQS reviews.

installed then removed and evaluated by trained personnel.  PM2.5 monitoring began in
1999 with all sites utilizing FRMs. By 2008, additional methods, known as Federal
Equivalent Methods (FEM)–began to be approved by EPA.

On February 7, 2024, the EPA promulgated a revised primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS, strengthening the standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM10 (coarse particle) standard at 150 µg/m3; and retained the current suite of secondary PM standards.  On October 2, 2026, EPA provided notice of its intended approach for finalizing designations for the revised 2024 annual PM2.5 NAAQS. View the intended designations for all States and Territories. Once designations are effective, they guide actions that States, territories, Tribes and the EPA must take to improve or preserve air quality in each area.  The EPA will work with the States and Tribes to share the responsibility of reducing fine particle pollution.

verdict.summary:
Current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5:

| Ask | Pollutant / averaging time | Primary standard level | Regulatory form |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 1 | PM2.5 annual | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 years; standard is met when the 3-year average annual arithmetic mean is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³. |
| 2 | PM2.5 24-hour | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years; standard is met when the 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile 24-hour concentrations is ≤ 35 µg/m³. |

Basis: EPA's February 7, 2024 final reconsideration of the PM NAAQS revised the primary annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³ and retained the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m³. The 2024 final rule is published at 89 FR 16202; EPA's PM NAAQS fact sheet and NAAQS page state the same levels. The 24-hour primary standard remains 35 µg/m³ under 40 CFR 50.18(c).

Source note: The eCFR §50.18 snippet supplied in the grounding reproduces the pre-2024 text: 12.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour, with a 2013 Federal Register citation. That text conflicts with EPA's 2024 final rule and fact sheets. I treat the 2024 final rule as the latest final action and therefore use 9.0 µg/m³ for the annual primary standard. If a requester's controlling legal text is the pre-2024 codification, the annual value would be 12.0 µg/m³; that is not the current level under the latest final rule identified.

Not asked but relevant for context: the secondary annual PM2.5 standard is 15.0 µg/m³, and the secondary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is 35 µg/m³. The primary standards are health-based; the secondary standards are welfare-based.

verdict.summary:
SAFETY ENGINEER'S WRITTEN DETERMINATION
Subject: Fall-protection trigger height for unprotected sides and edges on walking-working surfaces — US general industry (29 CFR 1910, Subpart D)

1. ANSWER
In general industry, a US employer must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

Threshold: 4 ft (1.2 m), measured from the walking-working surface to the lower level.

2. REGULATORY BASIS
- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) — the general duty for unprotected sides and edges: each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level must be protected from falling by one or more of the systems listed in section 3.
- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) — "Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed": the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by (i) guardrail systems, (ii) safety net systems, or (iii) personal fall protection systems.
- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) — where the employer can demonstrate that use of these systems is not feasible or would create a greater hazard, the employer must develop and implement a written fall protection plan specifying the alternative measures and procedures.
- Supporting definitions and criteria: 29 CFR 1910.21 (definitions, including "walking-working surface" and "unprotected side or edge"), 1910.29 (design, performance and use criteria for guardrails, safety nets, personal fall protection, designated areas, ladder safety systems), 1910.30 (training).

3. COMPLIANT MEANS OF PROTECTION (general 4 ft case)
Any one or more of the following, meeting 1910.29 criteria:
(a) Guardrail system — top rail 42 in +/- 3 in, midrail, 200 lb load, capable of withstanding the specified forces, no openings that permit passage of a 19 in sphere where required.
(b) Safety net system — installed as close as practicable under the surface, with the specified drop/outward reach and load ratings, inspected and certified per 1910.29(c).
(c) Personal fall protection system — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system, with compatible full-body harness, anchorage rated per 1910.140 (e.g., 5,000 lb per employee attached, or engineered equivalent), and prompt rescue capability.

4. IMPORTANT EXCEPTIONS AND LOWER/EQUIVALENT TRIGGERS IN THE SAME SECTION (do not apply the 4 ft figure blindly)
(a) Dangerous equipment — 1910.28(b)(6). An employee less than 4 ft above dangerous equipment must still be protected from falling into or onto it by a guardrail system or travel restraint system, unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard. At 4 ft or more above dangerous equipment, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest is required. Practical effect: over dangerous equipment the duty is effectively continuous from any height, not only at 4 ft.
(b) Openings — 1910.28(b)(7). Where the inside bottom edge of an opening is less than 39 in (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and the outside bottom edge is 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest is required.
(c) Runways and similar walkways — 1910.28(b)(5). Guardrail system required at 4 ft (1.2 m) or more; a one-sided guardrail may be omitted only for a special-purpose runway at least 18 in (46 cm) wide with personal fall arrest or travel restraint used.
(d) Stairway landings — 1910.28(b)(11)(i). Unprotected side or edge of a stairway landing 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level requires a guardrail or stair rail system. Stair flights with at least 3 treads and at least 4 risers require stair rail systems and handrails regardless of height.
(e) Rope descent systems — 1910.28(b)(12)(ii). Personal fall arrest system required at 4 ft (1.2 m) or more.
(f) Low-slope roofs — 1910.28(b)(13). Trigger is distance from the roof edge, not height: within 6 ft (1.6 m) of the edge, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest; from 6 ft (1.6 m) to less than 15 ft (4.6 m), the same systems (designated area allowed for work that is both infrequent and temporary); 15 ft (4.6 m) or more from the edge, a designated area plus a work rule prohibiting employees within 15 ft (4.6 m) of the edge without fall protection.
(g) Repair pits, service pits, assembly pits — 1910.28(b)(8). Pits less than 10 ft deep are addressed by the section's specific provisions rather than the generic 4 ft rule; verify the applicable paragraph for the specific pit configuration.
(h) Fixed ladders — 1910.28(b)(9). Governed by the ladder-specific provisions (personal fall arrest or ladder safety system requirements at the heights stated there), not by (b)(15).
(i) Scaffolds — 1910.28(b)(12)(i) defers to 29 CFR part 1926 subpart L (construction scaffold rules).
(j) Slaughtering facility platforms — 1910.28(b)(14). Guardrail or travel restraint at 4 ft (1.2 m) or more on the unprotected working side.

5. SCOPE NOTE — CONSTRUCTION CONTRAST (not the answer)
Construction work governed by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M uses a different trigger (1926.501(b)(1): 6 ft (1.8 m) to a lower level for unprotected sides and edges). That figure does not apply to general industry and must not be substituted into the answer above. Shipyard (1915), longshoring (1917), and agriculture (1928) have their own thresholds. If the workplace is a mixed-operation site, determine which part's standard governs the specific task before selecting a threshold.

6. STATE-PLAN NOTE
Federal OSHA sets the floor. The 26 states and 2 territories with OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as federal OSHA but may adopt different (stricter or differently structured) walking-working-surface rules, and a few have not adopted the current 1910.28 text verbatim. Before applying the 4 ft (1.2 m) figure at a specific site in a State Plan jurisdiction, confirm the state's adopted rule. In federal-jurisdiction states the figure above governs.

7. IMPLEMENTATION CHECKLIST FOR THE EMPLOYER
1) Identify every walking-working surface and mark those with an unprotected side or edge 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
2) Measure to the lower level actually present; also screen for dangerous equipment below (which triggers protection below 4 ft), openings, pits, roof-edge work distance, fixed ladders, and scaffolds — each may impose a different or additional duty.
3) Select a system from section 3 (or the section-specific list for the exception in section 4) that meets 1910.29 criteria.
4) Where no system is feasible or a system creates a greater hazard, prepare and implement the written fall protection plan required by 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) (or the equivalent paragraph-specific infeasibility provision, e.g., 1910.28(b)(14)(ii)).
5) Train each exposed employee per 1910.30 on the nature of the hazard, the systems used, correct use and limitations, inspection, and rescue; retrain on change or demonstrated deficiency.
6) Inspect and maintain guardrails, nets, harnesses, lanyards, anchorages, and ladder safety systems per 1910.29 and 1910.140; document inspections and any certification required for safety nets.
7) Provide prompt rescue for anyone using a personal fall arrest system.

8. LIMITS OF THIS DETERMINATION
This determination states the regulatory threshold and the associated duties under the current 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D text as published in the eCFR and in the 2018, 2024 and 2025 print editions of 29 CFR. It is a compliance-threshold answer, not a site-specific hazard analysis; the actual system selection, anchorage design, clearance calculations, and rescue plan for a given location require a qualified person's evaluation of that location.

(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—




(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or






(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.







(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter (rotorcraft) beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and then, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly for **at least 20 minutes** beyond that point. The 20-minute figure applies **day and night**; there is no night increase for rotorcraft.

Regulatory basis: 14 CFR § 91.151(b) —

> "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

## 1. Applicability and scope

| Item | Determination |
|---|---|
| Rule | 14 CFR § 91.151(b), Part 91 Subpart B (flight rules) |
| Aircraft | Rotorcraft (helicopter; also gyroplane, which 14 CFR 1.1 classifies as rotorcraft) |
| Flight conditions | VFR |
| Time of day | No distinction — 20 min applies day and night |
| Regime | US civil operations under Part 91. Commercial helicopter VFR under Part 135 has the **same** 20-minute reserve (§ 135.209(b); AC 194-1 § 5.7.1: "helicopters must have enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing ... and to fly after that for at least 20 minutes regardless of day or nighttime") |
| Not applicable here | Airplane VFR reserves (30 min day / 45 min night, § 91.151(a)); IFR reserves (45 min fixed-wing / 30 min helicopter, § 91.167(a)(3)); alternate-airport fuel (no VFR alternate fuel requirement in Part 91) |

Because both Part 91 and Part 135 helicopter VFR prescribe 20 minutes, the answer does not depend on resolving whether the flight is a commercial operation — a useful robustness property.

## 2. What the 20 minutes is and is not

- It is **flight time at normal cruising speed**, not hover time, not loiter, and not a fixed volume.
- It is **in addition to** the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing, computed **considering wind and forecast weather conditions** — i.e., the en-route leg must be planned into a headwind, and the 20 minutes is then applied on top.
- It is a **minimum**. Company policy, an operator's operations specifications, a letter of authorization, or pilot judgment under § 91.103 (preflight action: "fuel required") may require more. Known ATC delays or forecast conditions that would extend the flight must be accounted for.
- It is measured in **usable fuel** — fuel that cannot be accessed in flight does not count toward the reserve.
- It is a **takeoff** requirement: the fuel must be aboard when the flight begins, not averaged over the flight.
- It does **not** include taxi/startup/run-up allowance; that is a separate planning increment on top of (en-route fuel + 20-minute reserve).

## 3. Converting 20 minutes to a quantity of fuel

No aircraft performance data was supplied, so the regulation's own unit — minutes — is the answer. To turn it into gallons or pounds for a specific helicopter:

**Step 1 — establish normal cruising speed fuel burn.** Use the cruise fuel-consumption figure (gal/hr) from the rotorcraft flight manual at the planned cruise power setting and altitude, and use the **highest** (worst-case) value across the cruise band you will actually use, not an averaged or best-economy figure.

**Step 2 — compute the reserve:**

```
Reserve (gal) = Cruise burn (gal/hr) x (20 / 60) = Cruise burn / 3
Reserve (lb)  = Reserve (gal) x fuel density
                (100LL avgas ~6.0 lb/gal; Jet A/A-1 ~6.7 lb/gal)
```

**Step 3 — compute total fuel at start:**

```
Total required = Trip fuel to first point of intended landing (wind-adjusted)
               + Reserve (20 min at normal cruise)
               + Taxi / start / run-up allowance
               + Any contingency for known delays or forecast conditions
```

**Step 4 — verify it fits:** confirm Total required <= usable fuel capacity, and that the reserve is contained within usable (not total) fuel.

Illustrative worked values (examples only — substitute the actual aircraft's flight-manual burn):

| Normal-cruise burn | Reserve, 20 min (gal) | Approx. reserve (lb, avgas) |
|---|---|---|
| 8.5 gph (e.g., light two-seat piston trainer class) | 2.8 | ~17 |
| 13 gph (e.g., four-seat piston class) | 4.3 | ~26 |
| 25 gph (e.g., light turbine single) | 8.3 | ~50 |
| 40 gph (e.g., medium turbine single) | 13.3 | ~80 |

Each figure is exactly burn/3; none is a regulatory minimum, and the regulatory minimum remains 20 minutes regardless of the resulting volume.

## 4. Common errors this answer guards against

1. Applying the airplane numbers (30 min day / 45 min night) to a helicopter — wrong; § 91.151(a) is airplanes only.
2. Applying a night penalty to a helicopter — the rotorcraft rule has no day/night split.
3. Applying the 30-minute helicopter **IFR** reserve (§ 91.167(a)(3)) to a VFR flight — wrong rule; that is an IFR requirement.
4. Planning 20 minutes at hover or loiter burn instead of normal cruising speed — overstates the reserve and can be unachievable in a low-fuel state; the rule says normal cruising speed.
5. Counting total fuel rather than usable fuel.
6. Treating 20 minutes as the whole fuel plan — it is the increment after the en-route fuel, and § 91.103 still requires accounting for wind, forecast weather, and known delays.

## 5. What would change the answer

- **Powered-lift** certificated to conduct Copter procedures with vertical-lift landing capability for the entire route may use the helicopter VFR minimums (20 min) under the authority discussed in AC 194-1 (§ 194.306(ss)); otherwise airplane minimums apply.
- **IFR** instead of VFR: 45 min normal cruise, or 30 min for helicopters, under § 91.167(a)(3), plus alternate fuel if required.
- **Non-US registry / foreign authority**, or **public aircraft** outside Part 91: different or no rule — outside this answer.
- **Stricter operator, opspec, or company manual** value: governs over the regulatory floor.

## 6. Bottom line

20 minutes at normal cruising speed, day or night, beyond the fuel to reach the first point of intended landing — 14 CFR § 91.151(b), and identically 20 minutes under § 135.209(b) for Part 135 helicopter VFR.

RFC 8996
Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo

registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447], which indicates that such entries are not
recommended by the IETF.¶
The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.¶
The authentication of the peers depends on SHA-1 signatures.¶

Best Current Practice
R. Salz
N. Aviram
July 2026
IETF publication
Security Area
Show abstract
Abstract
TLS 1.3 is widely used, has had comprehensive security proofs, and improves both security and privacy deficiencies in TLS 1.2. Therefore, new protocols that use TLS must require TLS 1.3. As DTLS 1.3 is not widely available or deployed, this prescription does not pertain to DTLS (in any DTLS version); it pertains to TLS only.
This document updates RFC 9325. It discusses post-quantum cryptography and the security and privacy improvements in TLS 1.3 as the rationale for the update.

RFC 8996:   BCP 195: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
Best Current Practice
K. Moriarty
S. Farrell
March 2021
IETF publication
Security Area
Show abstract
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status. These versions lack support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and various government and industry profiles of applications using TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2 became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008 (subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing sufficient time to transition away from older versions. Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and streamlines library and product maintenance.
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1.

Received changes through RFC Editor sync (created alias RFC 8996, changed title to 'Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1', changed abstract to 'This document …
Received changes through RFC Editor sync (created alias RFC 8996, changed title to 'Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1', changed abstract to 'This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status. These versions lack support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and various government and industry profiles of applications using TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2 became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008 (subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing sufficient time to transition away from older versions. Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and streamlines library and product maintenance.
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1.

verdict.summary:
ANSWERS

1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is **RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; IETF, Security Area; part of BCP 195).

2. It gave the RFCs that had defined those versions **Historic** status — i.e., it moved them to Historic. The two defining documents are RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1).

SUPPORTING QUOTES (RFC 8996, Abstract)

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

RFC 8996, Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

STRUCTURED REFERENCE ENTRY

  Deprecating document : RFC 8996
  Title                : Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
  Authors              : K. Moriarty, S. Farrell
  Date                 : March 2021 (RFC Editor publication date 2021-03-23)
  Stream / series      : IETF; BCP 195 ("This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice")
  Action               : Formal deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1
  Status change applied: RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) -> Historic; RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) -> Historic
  DOI                  : 10.17487/RFC8996
  URL                  : https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996

SCOPE DETAIL WORTH CARRYING ALONGSIDE THE ANSWER

- DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) is deprecated by the same document and was likewise moved to Historic. DTLS 1.2 is explicitly *not* deprecated (and there is no DTLS 1.1).
- One additional RFC was moved to Historic as a consequence: RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites), because the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic.
- RFC 8996 updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1, and it updates RFC 7525 (the prior TLS-usage best-practice document); that is why it is part of BCP 195. BCP 195 was later revised by RFC 9325 (November 2022).
- Terminology note (the plan flagged this as a likely point of confusion): "deprecated," "obsoleted," and "moved to Historic" are distinct IETF actions. RFC 8996 *deprecates* TLS 1.0/1.1; the defining documents were *moved to Historic* by the status-change action; they were earlier *superseded* (obsoleted) by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) in 2008, not by RFC 8996. So the correct phrasing is: RFC 8996 deprecated the protocol versions and moved RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 to Historic status — it did not obsolete them.
- Practical consequence for compliance/security readers: TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 should not be used; TLS 1.2 or later is required (TLS 1.3 recommended).

CAVEAT (does not affect either answer)

A reference list in a later document (RFC 10015) cites RFC 9846 as "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3" (July 2026), whereas RFC 8996 cites RFC 8446 as TLS 1.3. This discrepancy concerns TLS 1.3's defining RFC only and has no bearing on which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0/1.1 or on the Historic status assigned to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346.

VERIFICATION

- Ask 1 value, "RFC 8996", is corroborated independently by the RFC 8996 title page, its Abstract, the RFC Editor's BCP 195 index page ("RFC 8996: BCP 195: Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 ... March 2021"), the RFC 8996 XML, and the Datatracker history page.
- Ask 2 value, "Historic", is the exact status term used in both the Abstract and Section 1 of RFC 8996 ("moved to Historic status"), and it is the IETF status-change terminology rather than a paraphrase.
- No numeric thresholds, bounds, or computed figures appear in this deliverable, so no stated value can conflict with a limit set elsewhere in it.

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each. Thus,
an individual with wages equal to or larger than $192,300 would contribute $11,922.60
to the OASDI program in 2027, and his or her employer would contribute the same
amount. The OASDI tax rate for self-employment income in 2027 is 12.4 percent.

Contribution and Benefit Base Determination
Automatic Determinations
Contribution & Benefit Base
Wage-indexed Amounts
Method for determining the base
The formula for determining the OASDI contribution and benefit base
is set by law. The formula is applicable only if a
cost-of-living increase becomes
effective for December of the year in which a determination of
the base would ordinarily be made.  Because there is a cost-of-living increase for December 2026, the
formula is applicable.  The formula states that the base for any year
Y after 1994 is equal to the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by
the ratio of the national average wage index for
year (Y-2) to that for 1992, with the result rounded to the nearest
multiple of $300.  If the result is less than the current base, the base
is not reduced.
Base for 2027
Under the above formula, the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600
multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for
1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500.  If the amount so determined
is not a multiple of $300, it is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.

To update a 2025 version of the calculator, choose
Properties from the main menu, then Historical
Amounts, then Update. If the dialog box that appears
requests amounts for 2026, enter the above amounts.
If it requests amounts for 2027 or later, then the
amounts for 2026 computations have already been entered. In that
case, press Cancel, then choose Properties,
Historical Amounts, and Modify. In the dialog box
that appears, press Next Year or Previous Year
until it requests amounts for 2026 computations. Then enter the above
amounts.

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.
The OASDI tax rate for wages paid in
2027 is set by statute at 6.2 percent for employees and employers, each. Thus,
an individual with wages equal to or larger than $192,300 would contribute $11,922.60
to the OASDI program in 2027, and his or her employer would contribute the same
amount. The OASDI tax rate for self-employment income in 2027 is 12.4 percent.

verdict.summary:
The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum, i.e., the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

Authority and confirmation:
- SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html): the annual table gives 2025 = $176,100, 2026 = $184,500, 2027 = $192,300. The page explains that the limit changes each year with the national average wage index and is commonly called the taxable maximum.
- SSA, Updating the Social Security Benefit Calculator (https://www.ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html): 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500.' The same page lists the 2026 'old-law' base as $137,100, a separate figure used in certain benefit computations and not the payroll-tax cap.
- SSA, Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026 (https://www.ssa.gov/policy/docs/chartbooks/fast_facts/2026/fast_facts26.html): 'Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026' — OASDI 184,500; HI No limit.
- SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 (https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf): Social Security wages and tips 'should not exceed the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026),' and Social Security tax withheld 'should not exceed $11,439.00 for tax year 2026.'

Arithmetic cross-check: the employee OASDI rate is 6.2 percent, and 184,500 x 0.062 = 11,439.00, matching the EFW2 maximum withholding figure exactly. Employer rate is also 6.2 percent (maximum $11,439.00 each); the self-employed OASDI rate is 12.4 percent (maximum $22,878.00). Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI) has no wage cap in 2026.

Scope note: this is the cap on earnings for the Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax for wages paid in calendar year 2026. It is not the Medicare wage base (uncapped) and not the 'old-law' base ($137,100). The figure was set by the automatic adjustment formula under 42 U.S.C. § 430 using the national average wage index and announced by SSA in fall 2025; it is therefore an official determination, not an estimate.

Your plan's terms may impose a lower limit on elective deferrals.
If you are a manager, owner, or highly compensated employee, your plan might need to limit your deferrals to pass nondiscrimination tests.
Catch-up contributions for those age 50 and over
If permitted by the 401(k) plan, participants age 50 or over at the end of the calendar year can also make catch-up contributions. You may contribute additional elective salary deferrals of:
$8,000 in 2026 to traditional and safe harbor 401(k) plans. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 or 63 who participate in these plans. For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $11,250.
$4000 in 2026 to SIMPLE 401(k) plans. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 or 63 who participate in SIMPLE plans. For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $5,250.
These amounts are subject to cost-of-living adjustments.
You don’t need to be “behind” in your plan contributions in order to be eligible to make these additional elective deferrals.

Example 2:  In Example 1, if Greg were 52 years old and eligible to make catch-up contributions, he could contribute an additional $6,500 of elective deferrals for 2020. His catch-up contribution could be split between the plans in any proportion he chooses. Or, Greg may contribute the full $6,500 catch-up contribution to his solo 401(k) plan, making a total contribution of $63,500 for 2020. Compensation limit for contributions
The amount of your compensation that can be taken into account when determining employer and employee contributions is limited to $360,000 for 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.

Elective deferral limits for 2025 and 2026. The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026. These limits apply for participants in SARSEPs, 401(k) plans (excluding SIMPLE plans), section 403(b) plans, and section 457(b) plans.
Defined contribution limits for 2025 and 2026. The limit on contributions, other than catch-up contributions, for a participant in a defined contribution plan is $70,000 for 2025 and increases to $72,000 for 2026.
Defined benefit limits for 2025 and 2026. The limit on annual benefits for a participant in a defined benefit plan is $280,000 for 2025 and increases to $290,000 for 2026.
SIMPLE plan salary reduction contribution limits for 2025 and 2026. The limit on salary reduction contributions, other than catch-up contributions, is $16,500 for 2025 and increases to $17,000 for 2026. Pursuant to section 117 of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022, a higher limit ($18,100 for 2025) may apply to participants in certain SIMPLE plans, effective for tax years beginning after 2023.

The catch-up contribution limit.
The excess of the participant's compensation over the elective deferrals that aren't catch-up contributions.
Catch-up contributions aren't subject to the elective deferral limit (the lesser of 25% of compensation, or $23,500 in 2025 and $24,500 in 2026).
Beginning in 2025, section 109 of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 permits a SARSEP to allow participants to make a higher amount of catch-up contributions in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63. For 2025 and 2026, the higher limit on catch-up contributions to a SARSEP for such participants is $11,2
quotes.whole:
The catch-up contribution limit.
The excess of the participant's compensation over the elective deferrals that aren't catch-up contributions.
Catch-up contributions aren't subject to the elective deferral limit (the lesser of 25% of compensation, or $23,500 in 2025 and $24,500 in 2026).
Beginning in 2025, section 109 of the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 permits a SARSEP to allow participants to make a higher amount of catch-up contributions in a tax year in which they attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63. For 2025 and 2026, the higher limit on catch-up contributions to a SARSEP for such participants is $11,250.
Overall limit on SEP contributions.
If you also make nonelective contributions to a SEP IRA, the total of the nonelective and elective contributions to that SEP IRA can't exceed the lesser of 25% of the employee's compensation, or $70,000 for 2025 ($72,000 for 2026). The same rule applies to contributions you make to your own SEP IRA. See Contribution Limits, earlier.
Figuring the elective deferral.
For figuring the 25% limit on elective deferrals, compensation doesn't include SEP contributions, including elective deferrals or other amounts deferred in certain employee benefit plans.

Under a qualified Roth contribution program, the amount of elective deferrals that an employee may designate as a Roth contribution is limited to the maximum amount of elective deferrals excludable from gross income for the year (for 2025, $23,500 if under age 50 and $31,000 if age 50 or over (but not attaining age 60, 61, 62, or 63); amounts increase in 2026 to $24,500 and $32,500, respectively) less the total amount of the employee's elective deferrals not designated as Roth contributions.
