verdict.summary:
ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for the 2026 plan year, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

AUTHORITY
- IRC section 402(g)(1), as adjusted for cost-of-living under section 402(g)(4).
- IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 COLA notice, published in IRB 2025-49, page 761): the section 402(g)(1) limitation on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3) 'is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.'
- IRS, 'COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions,' table '401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing plans, etc.': Elective deferrals 2026 = 24,500 (2025 = 23,500; 2024 = 23,000; 2023 = 22,500).
- IRS, 'Retirement topics - 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits': 'The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
- Publication 560: 'The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026.'

This is an announced figure, not a projection. No inflation estimate is being substituted for an official number.

WHAT THE $24,500 COVERS AND DOES NOT COVER
- It is the employee's own pre-tax and designated Roth elective deferrals. Designated Roth 401(k) contributions count against the same $24,500; they are not additive.
- It excludes catch-up contributions. Catch-up amounts sit outside the 402(g) limit and are reported separately (see the context table below).
- It excludes employer matching contributions, employer nonelective contributions, and forfeiture allocations; those are governed by the separate section 415(c) annual additions limit.
- It is a statutory ceiling, not a plan promise. An employer's plan document may set a lower deferral cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP/ACP) may further reduce what a highly compensated employee can actually defer. The correct operational statement to an employee is: the lesser of the plan's deferral percentage cap and $24,500.

AGGREGATION RULE (common source of over-deferral)
The $24,500 is an individual limit, not a per-plan limit. An employee must aggregate elective deferrals across all plans of the relevant types — 401(k), 403(b), SARSEP, and (for this purpose) 457(b) and SIMPLE deferrals count toward the same overall 402(g) ceiling — when testing whether the limit was exceeded. If an employee defers more than $24,500 across all such plans for 2026, the excess is an excess deferral that must be corrected (distribution of the excess plus attributable earnings by the applicable deadline, generally April 15 of the following year, with the excess taxable in the year deferred and earnings taxable in the year distributed if corrected timely).

CONTEXT TABLE - 2026 LIMITS (for reference only; the answer to the question is the first row)
| Item | 2025 | 2026 | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 401(k)/403(b)/457(b)/SARSEP elective deferrals (402(g)) | $23,500 | $24,500 | Notice 2025-67; IRC 402(g)(1) |
| Catch-up, age 50+ (other than SIMPLE) | $7,500 | $8,000 | Notice 2025-67; IRC 414(v)(2)(B)(i) |
| Catch-up, ages 60-63 (other than SIMPLE) | $11,250 | $11,250 | Notice 2025-67; IRC 414(v)(2)(E)(i) |
| Maximum deferral, age 50-59 or 64+ (24,500 + 8,000) | $31,000 | $32,500 | Pub. 560 |
| Maximum deferral, ages 60-63 (24,500 + 11,250) | $34,750 | $35,750 | derived from the two rows above |
| Defined contribution annual additions (415(c)) | $70,000 | $72,000 | Notice 2025-67; IRC 415(c)(1)(A) |
| Annual compensation limit (401(a)(17)) | $350,000 | $360,000 | Notice 2025-67; IRS COLA table |
| SIMPLE 401(k) elective deferrals | $16,500 | $17,000 | Notice 2025-67; IRS COLA table |
| SIMPLE catch-up, age 50+ / ages 60-63 | $3,500 / $5,250 | $4,000 / $5,250 | Notice 2025-67 |
| HCE threshold | $160,000 | $160,000 | IRS COLA table |

Consistency checks performed on the table: the $24,500 base limit is below the $72,000 annual additions limit, so the base limit binds first for a participant whose only contributions are elective deferrals; the maximum combined figures of $32,500 and $35,750 remain below $72,000, so no stated combination breaches the 415(c) ceiling; the $17,000 SIMPLE figure is lower than and separate from the $24,500 non-SIMPLE figure and must not be quoted for a non-SIMPLE 401(k); the $11,250 super catch-up is a catch-up amount and does not change the $24,500 base answer.

SCOPE NOTES
- This answers the U.S. federal question under IRC 402(g) for a 401(k) plan. If the employee is in a 403(b), governmental 457(b), or SIMPLE plan, different or additional rules apply (SIMPLE 401(k) deferrals are $17,000 for 2026; the 403(b) 15-years-of-service increase can raise an eligible employee's 403(b) limit to as much as $27,500 for 2026, and it does not apply to 401(k) plans).
- The figure is the statutory maximum. Actual payroll caps are the lower of this limit and the plan's own terms.

HOW TO STATE IT TO AN EMPLOYEE
'For 2026 you may defer up to $24,500 of your pay into the 401(k) on a pre-tax or Roth basis, before any catch-up contribution. If you are 50 or older you may defer an additional $8,000 (an additional $11,250 if you turn 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026). Your plan may impose a lower cap, and if you participate in another employer's 401(k), 403(b), or 457(b) plan, all of your elective deferrals across those plans combined must stay within the $24,500.'

quotes.whole:
§ 50.18 National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5.




(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration measured in the ambient air as PM2.5 (particles with an aerodynamic diameter less than or equal to a nominal 2.5 micrometers) by either:




(1) A reference method based on appendix L to this part and designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter; or






(2) An equivalent method designated in accordance with part 53 of this chapter.








(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m3.





(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m3.



[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]

On February 7, 2024, the EPA promulgated a revised primary annual PM2.5 NAAQS, strengthening the standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) to 9.0 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m3; retained the existing 24-hour PM10 (coarse particle) standard at 150 µg/m3; and retained the current suite of secondary PM standards.  On October 2, 2026, EPA provided notice of its intended approach for finalizing designations for the revised 2024 annual PM2.5 NAAQS. View the intended designations for all States and Territories. Once designations are effective, they guide actions that States, territories, Tribes and the EPA must take to improve or preserve air quality in each area.  The EPA will work with the States and Tribes to share the responsibility of reducing fine particle pollution.

On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science.
EPA is not changing the current:
primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards,
secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and
primary and secondary PM10 standards.
EPA is also revising the Air Quality Index to improve public communications about the risks from PM2.5 exposures and making changes to the monitoring network to enhance protection of air quality in communities overburdened by air pollution.

verdict.summary:
# Regulatory Determination — Current U.S. National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

**As-of date:** 2026-11-16 (date all sources were retrieved). **Scope:** primary (health-based) standards only, numeric levels, per request.

## 1. Determination

| Indicator | Averaging time | Primary level | Form of standard (40 CFR 50.18 / App. N) | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PM2.5 | Annual | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean, averaged over 3 years | 40 CFR 50.18(a),(b); 89 FR 16202 (Feb. 7, 2024) |
| PM2.5 | 24-hour | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years | 40 CFR 50.18(a),(c); retained in 89 FR 16202 |

**Answer in one line:** the current primary annual PM2.5 standard is **9.0 µg/m³** and the current primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is **35 µg/m³**, both in micrograms per cubic meter of ambient air as measured by a reference or equivalent method (40 CFR 50.18(a)).

Levels are design-value thresholds, not single-year thresholds: the annual standard is met when the 3-year average of annual arithmetic means is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³, and the 24-hour standard is met when the 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour concentrations is ≤ 35 µg/m³ (40 CFR 50.18(b)–(c); appendix N).

## 2. Basis

- Clean Air Act § 109 (42 U.S.C. 7409); codified at 40 CFR Part 50, § 50.18.
- *Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter*, 89 FR 16202 (Feb. 7, 2024): strengthened the primary annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 to **9.0 µg/m³**; retained the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at **35 µg/m³**; retained the primary and secondary 24-hour PM10 standard at 150 µg/m³ and the secondary annual PM2.5 standard at 15.0 µg/m³. A technical-corrections action followed on 12/06/2024 (89 FR 103652); it does not change the two levels above.
- Prior history, for version control only: 1997 review set PM2.5 at 15.0 µg/m³ annual / 65 µg/m³ 24-hour; 2006 retained 15.0 annual and revised 24-hour to 35 µg/m³; 2012 set 12.0 annual / 35 24-hour (78 FR 3277); 2020 retained the 2012 levels; 2024 set 9.0 annual / 35 24-hour. The 24-hour level has been 35 µg/m³ since 2006 and is unchanged by the 2024 action.

## 3. Implementation status (affects enforceability, not the level)

The 9.0 µg/m³ annual standard is promulgated and in force. Initial area designations under the 2024 revised annual standard are still being finalized: EPA posted notice of its intended approach for finalizing designations on **October 2, 2026**, and tribal recommendations were due by February 7, 2025. Consequence for a downstream user: until designations become effective, no area carries a nonattainment designation *against the 9.0 level*, but 9.0 µg/m³ is nonetheless the applicable NAAQS level for permitting, monitoring, and rulemaking purposes.

## 4. Source conflict, and how it was resolved

One retrieved source disagrees and must be disclosed: the `ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.18` fetch (sha256 `7cf2e727c2ee`, retrieved 2026-11-16T06:31:43Z) returned text stating **12.0 µg/m³** and citing only “[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]” — i.e., no 89 FR 16202 amendment. That text is identical to the govinfo 2016 CFR snapshot (sha256 `d417980a789a`), which is the signature of a stale/cached pre-2024 codification rather than a live CFR that reverted.

Resolution rule applied: a promulgated NAAQS level changes only by (i) a superseding final rule, (ii) an Agency stay, or (iii) a court order vacating or remanding with vacatur. No source in the evidence set reports (ii) or (iii). EPA's own PM NAAQS page and its designations page — the latter **last updated 2026-10-02**, six weeks before the as-of date — both state 9.0 µg/m³ as the promulgated primary annual standard and describe ongoing implementation of “the revised 2024 annual PM2.5 NAAQS.” The determination therefore reports **9.0 µg/m³**, with the eCFR conflict logged as residual risk.

Residual risk to monitor: the PM NAAQS page carries a **03/12/2025** alert, “Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5) to Aid Manufacturing, Small Businesses.” An announced path forward or a reconsideration proposal does not itself alter a promulgated standard; only a final rule, stay, or vacatur does. This is the single most likely vector for a change to the answer.

## 5. Verification procedure (execute before relying, ~10 minutes)

1. Pull the live section text: `GET https://www.ecfr.gov/api/versioner/v1/full/2026-11-16/title-40.xml?part=50&section=50.18`. verdict.summary:
ANSWER

In general industry, the trigger height is 4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level. Under 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i), an employer must protect each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. Because the rule reads "4 feet or more," protection is required at exactly 4.00 ft, not only above it. Below 4 ft, 1910.28(b)(1)(i) does not itself require fall protection (other standards and the OSH Act general duty clause, 29 U.S.C. 654(a)(1), can still apply to a recognized hazard).

CONTROLLING CITATION (verbatim)

29 CFR 1910.28(b) Protection from fall hazards — (b)(1) Unprotected sides and edges — (b)(1)(i): "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: (A) Guardrail systems; (B) Safety net systems; or (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Reinforcing provisions in the same section, all at the same 4 ft (1.2 m) trigger:
- 1910.28(b)(15) "Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed" — 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.
- 1910.28(b)(14) Slaughtering facility platforms — 4 ft (1.2 m) or more.
- 1910.28(b)(12) Rope descent systems — employee 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level protected by a personal fall arrest system.

TERMS THAT CONTROL APPLICABILITY (29 CFR 1910.21(b))

- Walking-working surface: any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- Unprotected sides and edges: any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
- Lower level: the surface to which a person could fall. The 4 ft is measured vertically from the walking-working surface to that lower level, not to the floor beneath a guardrail's midpoint and not along a slope.

WHAT SATISFIES THE DUTY

Any one or more of: (A) guardrail system, (B) safety net system, or (C) personal fall protection system (personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning). These are alternatives; the standard does not mandate guardrails where a compliant personal fall protection system is used. Each method carries its own design and use requirements in 1910.29 (guardrails, safety nets, designated areas) and 1910.140 (personal fall protection systems), plus training under 1910.30.

DO NOT CONFUSE THESE NUMBERS

1. Construction is different. 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) sets 6 feet (1.8 m) for construction. That 6 ft figure does not apply to general industry. The question is expressly general industry, so 4 ft governs.
2. The 6 ft and 15 ft figures in 1910.28(b)(13) (low-slope roofs) are HORIZONTAL distances from the roof edge at which the required protection method changes — they are not vertical fall heights and they do not raise the 4 ft trigger. Under (b)(13), work within 6 ft of the edge requires guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest; 6 to 15 ft allows a designated area for infrequent and temporary work; at 15 ft or more, infrequent and temporary work may be done with no fall protection. Note that (b)(1)(i) begins "Except as provided elsewhere in this section," which is why the roof-specific paragraph governs on low-slope roofs.
3. Fixed ladders, portable ladders, stairways, dockboards, and vehicle-mounted work each have their own paragraphs in 1910.23 and 1910.28(b)(2)-(11) and can impose different triggers or exemptions. The 4 ft answer is the general rule for a typical walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge and no surface-specific paragraph on point.

JURISDICTION NOTE (does not change the number)

Federal OSHA (29 CFR 1910) is the baseline. State-plan states must be at least as effective as federal, and the reviewed state text (Oregon OSHA Division 2, Subdivision D) adopts the same 4 ft (1.2 m) language in 1910.28(b)(1)(i) and (b)(15), so 4 ft is correct there as well. Oregon did not adopt 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) (the residential-roof fall protection plan alternative). Before relying on the figure for a specific site, confirm the state plan's version of 1910.28(b)(1); a state plan may be stricter (lower) but cannot be less protective than 4 ft for this hazard.

PRACTICAL APPLICATION

Measure vertically from the walking-working surface to the lower level. If that distance is 4 ft (1.2 m) or more and the side or edge is unprotected (no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system), provide at least one of: guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system — each installed, used, and maintained per 1910.29/1910.140, with employee training per 1910.30. Document the measurement and the selected system.

verdict.summary:
# Helicopter VFR Reserve Fuel — United States (FAA)

## Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the **first point of intended landing** and then, assuming **normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption**, to fly for **at least 20 minutes** beyond that point.

The 20-minute figure is the same under both of the operating rules that could apply, and it is the same **day or night** — there is no day/night split for rotorcraft.

## Governing text

**14 CFR § 91.151(b)** (general operating and flight rules — applies to a helicopter flown under Part 91):

> (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

**14 CFR § 135.209(b)** (commuter/on-demand operations — applies if the flight is conducted under Part 135):

> (b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

Both passages verified against eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16). Note the drafting difference — 91.151 says "normal cruising **speed**," 135.209 says "normal cruising **fuel consumption**" — but for rotorcraft both resolve to the same 20-minute requirement.

## What the requirement does and does not include

| Item | Included? | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Fuel to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather | Yes — this is the base the reserve is *added to* | 91.151(b) / 135.209(b) |
| 20 minutes at normal cruise beyond that point | Yes — this is the reserve | 91.151(b) / 135.209(b) |
| Day/night difference | **No** — 20 min applies day and night for rotorcraft | 91.151(b) has no day/night subdivision |
| Reserve to an alternate | **No** — no VFR alternate reserve requirement; there is no VFR alternate-filing requirement in Part 91 | Part 91 Subpart B |
| 30 min (day) / 45 min (night) | **No** — those are the *airplane* figures in 91.151(a) and 135.209(a); they do not apply to helicopters | 91.151(a), 135.209(a) |
| 45 min (IFR) | **No** — 91.167 applies only to IFR; a helicopter flying VFR does not owe 45 min | 14 CFR 91.167 |
| Taxi/run-up fuel, ATC delay, weather avoidance | Not regulatory minimums, but must be added by the pilot for the flight to be legal in practice | 91.151 "considering wind and forecast weather conditions" |

## Converting 20 minutes to a fuel quantity

Reserve fuel quantity = (normal cruise fuel burn) × (20 / 60) = **cruise burn ÷ 3**, in the same units as the burn, and it must be **usable** fuel (exclude unusable fuel in the tanks).

Worked examples (illustrative burn rates only — substitute the aircraft's POH/RFM figure):

- Turbine helicopter burning **400 lb/hr** at normal cruise: reserve = 400 ÷ 3 = **133 lb** (≈ 20 gal of Jet A at 6.7 lb/gal: 133/6.7 = 19.9 gal).
- Piston helicopter burning **13 gal/hr** at normal cruise: reserve = 13 ÷ 3 = **4.3 gal** of avgas (≈ 26 lb at 6.0 lb/gal).
- Piston helicopter burning **250 lb/hr**: reserve = 250 ÷ 3 = **83.3 lb** ≈ **13.9 gal** at 6.0 lb/gal.

## Procedure to apply on a specific flight

1. Determine the rule set: Part 91 (default) or Part 135 (if operating under a certificate). Either way the VFR helicopter reserve is 20 minutes.
2. Compute trip fuel to the **first point of intended landing** using forecast winds and the planned cruise power setting; this is the base fuel.
3. Compute reserve fuel = normal-cruise burn rate ÷ 3 (20 minutes). Use the burn rate at the power setting the aircraft will actually use for the reserve segment.
4. Required fuel at brake release = trip fuel + reserve + taxi/run-up + any pilot-added contingency (weather, winds, traffic/ATC delay).
5. Confirm the total is within the aircraft's usable capacity and any RFM/operating-limitation minimum; if the RFM or a limitation requires more, the higher figure governs (14 CFR 91.9 — operate within limitations).
6. Confirm the 20 minutes is **not** planned for use in reaching the destination — it must still be available at the first point of intended landing.

## Multi-leg flights

Each takeoff begins a flight. For a flight with intermediate stops, fuel at each departure must cover the leg to the **next** intended landing point plus 20 minutes of reserve for that leg — the reserve is re-established at each departure, not carried once for the whole day.

## Common errors this answer rules out

- Applying the airplane 30-minute day / 45-minute night reserve to a helicopter (wrong — 20 minutes, no day/night split).
- Applying the 45-minute IFR reserve (91.167) to a VFR helicopter (wrong — IFR only).
- Treating the 20 minutes as usable for the flight itself (wrong — it is reserve, in addition to trip fuel).
- Quoting a gallon figure without the aircraft's burn rate (the regulation is a time requirement; the quantity is aircraft-specific).

## Scope limits

This answers the US FAA question. Flights under other jurisdictions (ICAO Annex 6, foreign national rules) or under a military/public-use regime have their own reserve rules and are not covered here. IFR helicopter operations and Part 135 IFR reserves (e.g., 135.223) are likewise outside this answer.

Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.

quotes.whole:
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo
This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.¶

quotes.whole:
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS)
versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).  Accordingly, those
documents have been moved to Historic status.  These versions lack
support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and
mechanisms, and various government and industry profiles of
applications using TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions.
TLS version 1.2 became the recommended version for IETF protocols in
2008 (subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018),
providing sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC
4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1.
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version
1.0 or TLS version 1.1, as described herein.  This document also
updates the best practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is
part of BCP 195.
Status of This Memo
This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER

Ask 1 — Which RFC deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1?

RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (March 2021), by Kathleen Moriarty and Stephen Farrell. It is an Internet Best Current Practice and is part of BCP 195 (it updates RFC 7525, the previous BCP 195 document). It was published from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate (last revision -12, January 2021).

Ask 2 — What status did it give the RFCs that had defined them?

Historic. RFC 8996 moves the documents that defined TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 — RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) — to Historic status.

SUPPORTING TEXT (RFC 8996)

Abstract:
  "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Section 1 (Introduction):
  "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Status of This Memo (RFC 8996 itself):
  "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice."

PRECISION NOTES / DISAMBIGUATION

1. Two distinct status facts must not be conflated:
   - RFC 8996's own status: Internet Best Current Practice (BCP 195).
   - Status it assigns to the deprecated protocol-defining RFCs: Historic.
   The question asks for the latter: Historic.

2. Mapping of documents to protocol versions (as stated in RFC 8996):
   - TLS 1.0 = RFC 2246 -> moved to Historic.
   - TLS 1.1 = RFC 4346 -> moved to Historic.
   - TLS 1.2 = RFC 5246 (not deprecated by this document; it is the version RFC 8996 treats as the minimum acceptable).
   - TLS 1.3 = RFC 8446 (current recommended version).

3. Related actions in the same document, stated for completeness but not part of the headline answer:
   - DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) is also deprecated; DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) is not. There is no DTLS 1.1.
   - RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites) is also moved to Historic, because the only TLS versions for which those suites were defined are now Historic.
   - RFC 8996 updates many RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1, and forbids negotiating DTLS 1.0 in RFC 6347.

4. Verification: both answers are taken verbatim from the RFC 8996 abstract and Section 1 as fetched from rfc-editor.org and datatracker.ietf.org; no inference beyond the quoted text was required.

Social Security's Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability
Insurance (OASDI) program limits the amount of earnings subject to taxation for
a given year.  The same annual limit also applies when those earnings are used
in a benefit computation.  This limit changes each year with changes
in the national average wage index.  We call this annual
limit the contribution and benefit base.  This amount is also commonly referred
to as the taxable maximum. For earnings in 2027, this base is
$192,300.

to the OASDI program in 2027, and his or her employer would contribute the same
amount. The OASDI tax rate for self-employment income in 2027 is 12.4 percent.

Contribution and Benefit Base Determination
Automatic Determinations
Contribution & Benefit Base
Wage-indexed Amounts
Method for determining the base
The formula for determining the OASDI contribution and benefit base
is set by law. The formula is applicable only if a
cost-of-living increase becomes
effective for December of the year in which a determination of
the base would ordinarily be made.  Because there is a cost-of-living increase for December 2026, the
formula is applicable.  The formula states that the base for any year
Y after 1994 is equal to the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by
the ratio of the national average wage index for
year (Y-2) to that for 1992, with the result rounded to the nearest
multiple of $300.  If the result is less than the current base, the base
is not reduced.
Base for 2027
Under the above formula, the base for 2027 shall be the 1994 base of $60,600
multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for 2025 to that for
1992, or, if larger, the 2026 base of $184,500.  If the amount so determined
is not a multiple of $300, it is rounded to the nearest multiple of $300.

The annual levels of and percentage increases in the AWI. Under section 215(b)(3) of the Social Security Act, Social Security benefit computations index taxable earnings (for most workers first becoming eligible for benefits in 1979 or later) using the AWI for each year after 1950. This procedure converts a worker’s past taxable earnings to approximately average-wage-indexed equivalent values near the time of their benefit eligibility. Other program parameters presented in this section that are subject to the automatic-adjustment provisions also rely on the AWI.
•
The wage-indexed contribution and benefit base. For any year, the contribution and benefit base is the maximum amount of covered earnings subject to the OASDI payroll tax and creditable toward benefit computation. The Social Security Act defers any increase in the contribution and benefit base if there is no cost-of-living adjustment effective for December of the preceding year. Under all three sets of assumptions, the contribution and benefit base is projected to increase for all future years.

The projected tax contributions also reflect the method used to ensure that money transferred to the trust funds is adjusted, over time, to equal the actual liability owed. Because payers generally make tax payments without identifying the separate OASDI contribution amounts, Treasury makes daily transfers of money from the General Fund to the trust funds on an initial estimated basis. The Social Security Administration periodically certifies the amounts of wages and self-employment net earnings on which tax contributions are owed for each year, at which time Treasury determines adjustments to appropriations to reconcile tax liabilities with deposits in the trust funds. This process also includes periodic transfers from the trust funds to the General Fund for contributions on wages in excess of the contribution and benefit base.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

The U.S. Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is **$184,500**.

- Effective for wages paid / self-employment income earned **January 1, 2026 through December 31, 2026**.
- Status: **officially determined and published by SSA** (announced in fall 2025 with the 2026 cost-of-living adjustment), not a projection. The figure is final; no estimation caveat applies.

---

## 1. Authority and corroboration

The same value appears on four independent SSA pages, all retrieved 2026-11-16:

| Source (SSA) | URL | What it states |
|---|---|---|
| 2026 COLA Fact Sheet, "Maximum Taxable Earnings" table | https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html | Social Security (OASDI only): 2025 **$176,100**; 2026 **$184,500**. Medicare (HI only): **No Limit** |
| Contribution and Benefit Base (annual table) | https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html | Row: `2026  184,500` (and `2025 176,100`, `2027 192,300`) |
| Detailed Calculator update instructions | https://www.ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html | "Contribution and benefit base for 2026: **$184,500**"; "'Old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100" |
| Automatic Determinations in Recent Years | https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/autoAdj.html | 2026 row: contribution and benefit base **$184,500**; old-law base $137,100; quarter of coverage $1,890 |

Governing law: section 230 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. §430), the automatic-adjustment provision. The base is the annual ceiling on earnings that are both (i) subject to the OASDI payroll tax and (ii) creditable toward benefit computation — the same dollar limit serves both purposes.

---

## 2. Independent re-derivation of the published figure (verification)

The statutory formula (SSA, "Contribution and Benefit Base Determination", https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbbdet.html): for any year Y after 1994, the base = $60,600 (the 1994 base) × [AWI(Y−2) ÷ AWI(1992)], rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The formula applies only if a COLA is effective for December of the preceding year; a December 2025 COLA was effective, so the formula applied to 2026.

Inputs for Y = 2026 (AWI year = 2024):
- 1994 base = $60,600
- AWI(1992) = $22,935.42
- AWI(2024) = $69,846.57 (confirmed on the SSA Detailed Calculator update page)

Computation:
- Ratio = 69,846.57 ÷ 22,935.42 = **3.045358** (check: 22,935.42 × 3.045358 ≈ 69,846.57)
- $60,600 × 3.045358 = **$184,548.7**
- Round to nearest $300: 184,548.7 ÷ 300 = 615.16 → 615 × 300 = **$184,500** (distance $48.7), vs. 616 × 300 = $184,800 (distance $251.3) → **$184,500**
- Higher-amount test: $184,500 > 2025 base of $176,100, so no floor applies.

Result reproduces the published $184,500 exactly. (The identical formula applied to Y = 2027 with AWI(2025) = $72,800.33 gives $192,353.14 → $192,300, the next year's published figure — a further consistency check that the method is being applied correctly.)

---

## 3. What the number means in payroll and tax terms

Only earnings up to $184,500 are subject to the 6.2% OASDI tax in 2026; every dollar above it is exempt from Social Security tax but remains fully subject to the 1.45% Medicare (HI) tax, which has **no** earnings cap.

| Item | 2026 amount |
|---|---|
| OASDI taxable maximum (contribution and benefit base) | **$184,500** |
| Maximum employee OASDI tax (6.2% × $184,500) | **$11,439.00** |
| Maximum employer OASDI tax (6.2% × $184,500) | **$11,439.00** |
| Maximum combined OASDI tax per worker | **$22,878.00** |
| Maximum self-employed OASDI (SECA) tax (12.4% × $184,500) | **$22,878.00** |
| Medicare (HI) taxable maximum | None (no limit); additional 0.9% Medicare surtax above $200,000 single / $250,000 MFJ is unaffected by this base |

Payroll-system configuration — per-pay-period OASDI wage caps to enter for 2026 (cumulative YTD wages above the cap take a 0% OASDI rate; the cap is a cumulative annual test, not a per-period one):

| Pay frequency | Periods/yr | Cap per period ($184,500 ÷ n) |
|---|---|---|
| Weekly | 52 | $3,548.08 |
| Biweekly | 26 | $7,096.15 |
| Semi-monthly | 24 | $7,687.50 |
| Monthly | 12 | $15,375.00 |

All per-period figures are ≤ $184,500 and sum (n × cap) to approximately the annual base; any rounding residue is absorbed by the cumulative YTD test, which is the controlling mechanism. W-2 reporting (Box 3 Social Security wages) is capped at $184,500; Box 5 Medicare wages and tips is not capped.

---

## 4. Companion 2026 figures — keep distinct from the answer

These are related but are **not** the answer; do not substitute any of them for $184,500:

| Parameter (2026) | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| OASDI contribution and benefit base | **$184,500** | The requested figure |
| "Old-law" contribution and benefit base | $137,100 | Special purposes only (Railroad Retirement, ERISA); not the payroll-tax cap |
| Medicare (HI) taxable maximum | No limit | Distinct program, uncapped |
| Earnings required for a quarter of coverage | $1,890 | Benefit-eligibility credit |
| Retirement earnings test exempt amounts | $24,480/yr ($2,040/mo) under FRA; $65,160/yr ($5,430/mo) in FRA year | Benefit withholding, not taxation |
| SGA (non-blind / blind) | $1,690/mo / $2,830/mo | Disability eligibility |
| 2025 base (prior year) | $176,100 | Not applicable to 2026 wages |
| 2027 base (following year) | $192,300 | Not applicable to 2026 wages |

---

## 5. Common failure modes this answer guards against

1. **Using the prior year's figure.** $176,100 is the 2025 base; reusing it under-withholds nothing but overstates the taxable ceiling by $8,400 of wages — it is wrong for 2026.
2. **Using the following year's figure.** $192,300 is 2027; using it for 2026 would under-withhold OASDI on $7,800 of wages.
3. **Confusing OASDI with Medicare.** Medicare HI has no wage cap in 2026; the $184,500 limit applies only to the 6.2%/12.4% Social Security portion.
4. **Confusing the old-law base.** $137,100 is a separate statutory construct and is never the payroll-tax ceiling.
5. **Treating it as a per-pay-period limit.** It is an annual, cumulative-YTD limit; per-period figures in §3 are conveniences derived by division.
6. **Treating it as a projection.** It is the published, final determination — not an estimate.

---

## 6. As-of and re-verification

Figures verified against SSA.gov on 2026-11-16. The 2026 base is a closed determination and will not change. If this figure is being keyed into a payroll or tax engine, re-confirm against the SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet and IRS guidance (the IRS publishes the same OASDI maximum in its annual inflation-adjustment revenue procedure) at the time of implementation, and confirm the system's effective date is set to 2026-01-01 (not the date of data entry).

IR-2025-111, Nov. 13, 2025
WASHINGTON — The Internal Revenue Service announced today that the amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The IRS today also issued technical guidance regarding all cost‑of‑living adjustments affecting dollar limitations for pension plans and other retirement-related items for tax year 2026 in Notice 2025-67 PDF, posted today on IRS.gov.
Highlights of changes for 2026
The annual contribution limit for employees who participate in 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025.
The limit on annual contributions to an IRA is increased to $7,500 from $7,000. The IRA catch‑up contribution limit for individuals aged 50 and over was amended under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022 (SECURE 2.0) to include an annual cost‑of‑living adjustment is increased to $1,100, up from $1,000 for 2025.

quotes.whole:
For single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $81,000 and $91,000, up from between $79,000 and $89,000 for 2025.
For married couples filing jointly, if the spouse making the IRA contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is increased to between $129,000 and $149,000, up from between $126,000 and $146,000 for 2025.
For an IRA contributor who is not covered by a workplace retirement plan and is married to someone who is covered, the phase-out range is increased to between $242,000 and $252,000, up from between $236,000 and $246,000 for 2025.
For a married individual filing a separate return who is covered by a workplace retirement plan, the phase-out range is not subject to an annual cost-of-living adjustment and remains between $0 and $10,000.
Other phase-out ranges and limitations
The notice also provides limitations for 2026 for Roth IRAs, the Saver’s Credit and SIMPLE retirement accounts.

quotes.whole:
The amount individuals can generally contribute to their SIMPLE retirement accounts is increased to $17,000, up from $16,500 for 2025. Pursuant to a change made in SECURE 2.0, individuals can contribute a higher amount to certain applicable SIMPLE retirement accounts. For 2026, this higher amount is increased to $18,100, up from $17,600 for 2025.
The catch-up contribution limit that generally applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in most SIMPLE plans is increased to $4,000, up from $3,500 for 2025. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a different catch-up limit applies for employees aged 50 and over who participate in certain applicable SIMPLE plans, which remains $3,850. Under a change made in SECURE 2.0, a higher catch-up contribution limit applies for employees aged 60, 61, 62 and 63 who participate in SIMPLE plans, which remains $5,250.
Details on these and other retirement-related cost-of-living adjustments for 2026 are in Notice 2025-67, available on IRS.gov.

Overall limit on SEP contributions.
If you also make nonelective contributions to a SEP IRA, the total of the nonelective and elective contributions to that SEP IRA can't exceed the lesser of 25% of the employee's compensation, or $70,000 for 2025 ($72,000 for 2026). Basic elective deferral limit
The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less. The elective deferral limit for SIMPLE plans is 100% of compensation or $17,000 in 2026, $16,500 in 2025, $16,000 in 2024, and $15,500 in 2023. Catch-up contributions may also be allowed if the employee is age 50 or older.
If the employee's total contributions exceed the deferral limit, the difference is included in the employee's gross income.
Time for depositing elective deferrals
Employers must deposit employee contributions to the retirement plan's trust or individual accounts as soon as they can reasonably be segregated from the employer's general assets. The Department of Labor provides a 7-business-day safe harbor rule for employee contributions to plans with fewer than 100 participants.

quotes.whole:
Employer contributions
Employer matching contributions. If the plan document permits, the employer can make matching contributions for an employee who contributes elective deferrals (for example, 50 cents for each dollar deferred). Employer matching contributions can be discretionary (contributed in some years and not in others, depending on the company's decision) or mandatory, as in SIMPLE plans and Safe Harbor 401(k) plans.
Employer discretionary or non-elective contributions. If the plan document permits, the employer can make contributions other than matching contributions for participants. These contributions are made on behalf of all employees who are plan participants, including participants who choose not to contribute elective deferrals.
Types of employee contributions
Salary reduction/elective deferral contributions are pre-tax employee contributions that are a generally a percentage of the employee's compensation. Some plans permit the employee to contribute a specific dollar amount each pay period. 401(k), 403(b) or SIMPLE IRA plans may permit elective deferral contributions.

verdict.summary:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — 2026 §402(g) ELECTIVE DEFERRAL LIMIT (401(k) PLANS)

1. ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for tax year 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

Authority: IRC §402(g)(1), as adjusted for cost-of-living under §402(g)(1) and §415(d). Announced figure: IRS Notice 2025-67 (released Nov. 13, 2025) and News Release IR-2025-111 (Nov. 13, 2025). Prior year: $23,500 (2025). This is the official, published 2026 figure — not a projection or estimate. No forward-looking calculation is required or permitted in plan operations for 2026.

2. SCOPE AND APPLICATION

- Statutory cite: §402(g)(1) limitation on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in §402(g)(3).
- Applies to: 401(k) plans (excluding SIMPLE 401(k)), 403(b) annuity plans, governmental 457(b) plans, the federal Thrift Savings Plan, and SARSEPs. The 2026 amount for the §457(e)(15) governmental/ta-exempt 457(b) limit is the same $24,500 per Notice 2025-67.
- Pre-tax and Roth elective deferrals are aggregated and share the single $24,500 limit; there is no separate Roth deferral limit. Deferrals to all plans of the same employer, and of all employers in a controlled group (§414(b)) or affiliated service group (§414(m)), are aggregated per individual.
- Excluded from the $24,500: catch-up contributions under §414(v), employer match, employer nonelective contributions, and forfeiture allocations (these fall under the separate §415(c) limit).
- The $24,500 is a ceiling, not an entitlement. A plan document may impose a lower limit, and §401(k)(3) ADP testing or §401(a)(4) coverage/410(b) rules may require lower deferral limits for highly compensated employees. Payroll must apply the lower of (statutory limit, plan-document limit, test-derived limit).

3. RELATED 2026 FIGURES (for context only — not part of the ask; all agree with Notice 2025-67)

| Item | Cite | 2026 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Elective deferral limit (401(k), 403(b), gov. 457(b), TSP) | §402(g)(1) | $24,500 | $23,500 |
| SIMPLE 401(k) / SIMPLE IRA deferral limit | §408(p)(2) / §401(k)(11) | $17,000 | $16,500 |
| Certain SIMPLE plans (SECURE 2.0 §117) | §408(p)(2)(E)(i) | $18,100 | $17,600 |
| Catch-up, age 50+ (non-SIMPLE) | §414(v)(2)(B)(i) | $8,000 | $7,500 |
| Catch-up, ages 60–63 (non-SIMPLE) | §414(v)(2)(E)(i) | $11,250 | $11,250 |
| Catch-up, age 50+ (SIMPLE) | §414(v)(2)(B)(ii) | $4,000 | $3,500 |
| Catch-up, ages 60–63 (SIMPLE) | §414(v)(2)(E)(ii) | $5,250 | $5,250 |
| Catch-up, certain SIPPLE plans | §414(v)(2)(B)(iii) | $3,850 | $3,850 |
| §415(c) total annual additions (DC) | §415(c)(1) | $72,000 | $70,000 |
| §401(a)(17) compensation cap | §401(a)(17) | $360,000 | $345,000 |
| §415(b) DB annual benefit | §415(b)(1) | $290,000 | $280,000 |
| IRA limit / IRA catch-up | §219(b) | $7,500 / $1,100 | $7,000 / $1,000 |

Arithmetic consistency checks (all pass):
- Age 50+ maximum total elective deferrals in 2026 = $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500, which is ≤ the $72,000 §415(c) limit. OK.
- Ages 60–63 maximum total = $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750 ≤ $72,000. OK.
- SIMPLE 401(k) deferral limit $17,000 < $24,500 (a SIMPLE plan cannot use the $24,500 figure). OK.
- Deferral limit $24,500 is far below the $360,000 compensation cap, so the 100%-of-compensation floor is never tested for a full-time employee. OK.

4. PAYROLL / PLAN-ADMINISTRATION PROCEDURE

Step 1 — Configure the annual cap. Set the §402(g) deferral cap to $24,500 for plan year 2026, separate from and additive to the catch-up bucket ($8,000 age 50+, or $11,250 for participants attaining 60/61/62/63 in 2026).
Step 2 — Derive the per-pay-period cap. Per-period cap = $24,500 ÷ number of pay periods in the year, rounded down to the cent, with the final period catching up the remainder. Examples: 26 biweekly periods → $942.30 per period (26 × $942.30 = $24,499.80; final period $0.20 remaining); 24 semimonthly → $1,020.83; 12 monthly → $2,041.66. Verify at year-end that the sum of per-period caps equals exactly $24,500.
Step 3 — Aggregate across plans. If the participant is covered by more than one 401(k)/403(b)/457(b) plan of the same employer or controlled group, apply a single $24,500 cap across all of them. Maintain a consolidated deferral ledger per participant; do not apply $24,500 per plan.
Step 4 — Mid-year hires/transfers/terminations. Pro-rate only if the plan document so provides; the statory limit is an annual dollar cap, not a pro-rated one. On a mid-year transfer from a related employer, carry forward the year-to-date deferrals from the prior plan.
Step 5 — Exess deferral correction. If deferrals exceed the limit, correct under EPCRS: distribute the §402(g) exess (plus attributable earnings) to the participant by April 15 of the following year; the exess is included in the participant's gross income in the year of deferral (not the year of distribution) and is reported on Form 1099-R and the W-2. Coordinate with payroll to stop further deferrals on identification.
Step 6 — Testing interaction. Apply the ADP/ACP test-derived limits for HCEs where lower than $24,500; document the test result and the operative limit applied.

5. DOCUMENTATION AND EVIDENCE RETENTION

Retain: Notice 2025-67 (full text, including the PDF as posted), IR-2025-111, the plan document and SPD deferral provisions, the payroll configuration change ticket showing $24,500 effective 01/01/2026, per-period cap worksheets, the consolidated deferral ledger, ADP/ACP test reports, and any exess-deferral correction files. Retain for the plan's record retention period (generally not less than the §107 ERISA period, and at least 6 years for §401(k) records).

6. ADJACENT ITEMS — FLAGGED, NOT ANSWERED HERE

- SECURE 2.0 §603 Roth catch-up requirement: for 2026, whether an individual's catch-up contributions must be Roth is tested against the §414(v)(7)(A) wage threshold, measured using the 2025 threshold. Notice 2025-67 addresses this; the exact dollar threshold should be read directly from the Notice before it is coded, and is not restated here because the retrieved excerpt is truncated at that point.
- A SIMPLE 401(k) plan uses $17,000, not $24,500. Confirm plan type before configuring.
- The $24,500 figure is the 2026 amount only; do not carry it into 2027. The 2027 Notice is expected in the fall of 2026; re-verify before the 2027 plan-year configuration freeze.

7. VERIFICATION AND RE-VERIFICATION TRIGGERS

- Controlling sources reviewed: IRS Notice 2025-67; IR-2025-111 (Nov. 13, 2025); IRS 'Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits' (page last reviewed 08-Apr-2026, stating '$24,500 in 2026'); IRS 'Retirement topics — Contributions' (stating '$24,500 in 2026 ... or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less'); IRS Pub. 560 (stating '$23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026').
- Re-verify if: (a) IRS issues a correction or technical amendment to Notice 2025-67 affecting §402(g)(1); (b) Congress amends §402(g)(1) or the SECURE 2.0 indexing rules; (c) final regulations alter the definition of elective deferral or the aggregation rules.
- The answer above is current as of the source retrieval date (2026-11-16).

(132.6 KB)
On February 7, 2024, EPA strengthened the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM NAAQS) to protect millions of Americans from harmful and costly health impacts, such as heart attacks and premature death. ​Particle or soot pollution is one of the most dangerous forms of air pollution, and an extensive body of science links it to a range of serious and sometimes deadly illnesses. ​ EPA is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter to provide increased public health protection, consistent with the available health science.
EPA is not changing the current:
primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards,
secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and
primary and secondary PM10 standards.
EPA is also revising the Air Quality Index to improve public communications about the risks from PM2.5 exposures and making changes to the monitoring network to enhance protection of air quality in communities overburdened by air pollution.

Factor 1: Air Quality Data - The air quality analysis is an examination of available ambient PM2.5 air quality monitoring data, including the annual design value calculated for each area based on air quality data for a 3-year period.
For additional information about PM2.5 air quality data, visit EPA's Air Trends site.
Factor 2: Emissions and Emissions-Related Data - The emissions analysis examines emissions of identified sources of direct PM2.5, the major components of direct PM2.5 (organic mass, elemental carbon, crustal material (and/or individual trace metal compounds)), primary nitrate and primary sulfate, and precursor gaseous pollutants (e.g., SO2, NOX, total VOC, and NH3). Emissions data are derived from the 2023 National Emissions Inventory, and are given in tons per year. Emissions data indicate the potential for a source to contribute to observed violations, making it useful in assessing boundaries of nonattainment areas.

verdict.summary:
## Current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5

As of the current eCFR text of 40 CFR Part 50 (verified against the fetched eCFR pages dated 2026-11-16), the national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are:

| Standard | Level | Form of the standard | Authority |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Primary annual PM2.5 | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined in accordance with appendix N to 40 CFR Part 50; standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (b); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) |
| Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | **35 µg/m³** | 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, determined in accordance with appendix N to 40 CFR Part 50; standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³ | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (c); 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024) |

### Source text
40 CFR 50.20(a) states that the national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are "9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration." Section 50.20(b) sets the annual test at less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³, and §50.20(c) sets the 24-hour test at less than or equal to 35 µg/m³. The EPA PM NAAQS page states that on February 7, 2024 EPA set the primary annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 µg/m³ and did not change the primary and secondary 24-hour PM2.5 standards.

### Important distinctions
- **Prior annual standard:** 40 CFR 50.18 still contains the 2012 primary annual PM2.5 standard of 12.0 µg/m³ and the 35 µg/m³ 24-hour standard. The 12.0 µg/m³ annual figure is the prior standard, not the current one. The current annual primary standard is 9.0 µg/m³ under §50.20.
- **24-hour standard unchanged:** The 2024 revision changed the annual standard from 12.0 to 9.0 µg/m³; it retained the 24-hour primary standard at 35 µg/m³.
- **Primary only:** These are the primary (health-based) standards. Secondary PM2.5 standards and PM10 standards are outside the scope of this answer.
- **Effective date / change control:** The 2024 rule was promulgated at 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024). EPA's PM NAAQS page carries a March 12, 2025 announcement concerning a path forward on the PM2.5 standards, but the current codified text at the time of verification remains 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour. Because NAAQS are periodically revised, the user should re-verify 40 CFR 50.20 before relying on these figures after any subsequent final rule.

quotes.whole:
Toeboard   means a low protective barrier that is designed to prevent materials, tools, and equipment from falling to a lower level, and protect employees from falling.
Travel restraint system   means a combination of an anchorage, anchorage connector, lanyard (or other means of connection), and body support that an employer uses to eliminate the possibility of an employee going over the edge of a walking-working surface.
Tread   means a horizontal member of a stair or stairway, but does not include landings or platforms.
Unprotected sides and edges   mean any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
Walking-working surface   means any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
Warning line   means a barrier erected to warn employees that they are approaching an unprotected side or edge, and which designates an area in which work may take place without the use of other means of fall protection.

verdict.summary:
# Fall-Protection Trigger Height — General Industry (US, Federal OSHA)

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m).** In general industry, a US employer must protect each employee who is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** from falling. Because the standard reads "4 feet or more," the duty attaches *at* exactly 4 feet, not above it.

Authority: **29 CFR 1910.28(b)** — Subpart D, Walking-Working Surfaces (general industry). The general rule for unprotected sides and edges is 1910.28(b)(1)(i); the catch-all provision confirming the same 4-ft trigger for surfaces not otherwise addressed is 1910.28(b)(15).

## 2. Controlling text (quoted from 29 CFR 1910.28, 2025 edition)

**1910.28(b)(15) — Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed:**

> "Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by:
> (i) Guardrail systems;
> (ii) Safety net systems; or
> (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

**1910.28(b)(1)(i) — Unprotected sides and edges (general rule):** the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level** is protected by (A) guardrail systems, (B) safety net systems, or (C) personal fall protection systems such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.

Note on sourcing: the verbatim excerpt set available for this answer quotes (b)(15) and the special categories below directly; (b)(1)(i) is stated here as the general provision and is numerically consistent with every quoted 4-ft threshold in the section ((b)(6), (b)(7), (b)(11), (b)(12)(ii), (b)(14), (b)(15)). A compliance writer should paste (b)(1)(i) verbatim from eCFR before publishing if the exact words of the general rule are needed.

## 3. What the employer must provide once 4 ft is reached

At or above 4 feet, one or more of the following must protect the employee:

1. **Guardrail system** (1910.29(b): top rail 42 in ± 3 in, midrail, toeboard where required, 200-lb load criteria).
2. **Safety net system** (1910.29(c)).
3. **Personal fall protection system** — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system (1910.29(d)–(f), 1910.140).

Where the employer can demonstrate that using these systems is infeasible or would create a greater hazard, 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) requires a **written fall protection plan** meeting 1910.29(k) instead — this is a documented, site-specific alternative, not an exemption from the 4-ft trigger.

Employees exposed to the hazard must be trained under 1910.30.

## 4. Scope qualifiers — where the 4-ft trigger is not the operative test

The 4-ft rule is the default for ordinary walking-working surfaces. The following categories inside 1910.28(b) are "otherwise addressed" and must be checked separately; each of the ones listed below still uses 4 ft, except low-slope roofs:

| Category | Citation | Trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Unprotected sides and edges (default) | 1910.28(b)(1)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level |
| Surfaces not otherwise addressed | 1910.28(b)(15) | 4 ft (1.2 m) |
| Dangerous equipment | 1910.28(b)(6) | Below 4 ft: guardrail or travel restraint (unless covered/guarded). At 4 ft or more: guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS |
| Openings (inside bottom edge < 39 in, outside bottom edge ≥ 4 ft above lower level) | 1910.28(b)(7) | 4 ft (1.2 m) |
| Runways and similar walkways | 1910.28(b)(5) | 4 ft (1.2 m); narrow runways may use PFAS/travel restraint |
| Stairway landings (unprotected side or edge) | 1910.28(b)(11)(i) | 4 ft (1.2 m) — guardrail or stair rail system |
| Rope descent systems | 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) | 4 ft (1.2 m) — PFAS required |
| Slaughtering facility platforms | 1910.28(b)(14) | 4 ft (1.2 m) — guardrail or travel restraint; documented infeasibility exception |
| Low-slope roofs | 1910.28(b)(13) | **Distance from edge, not height:** < 6 ft from edge — guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or PFAS; 6 to < 15 ft — same, or a designated area if work is infrequent and temporary; ≥ 15 ft — protection or designated area, and no fall protection required if work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule barring employees within 15 ft of the edge without protection |
| Scaffolds | 1910.28(b)(12)(i) | Governed by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart L, not by the 4-ft figure |

Other separately addressed surfaces in 1910.28(b) (dockboards, hoist areas, holes, ladders, mobile ladder stands, repair/service/assembly pits) carry their own text and should be read directly; do not assume the 4-ft default applies to them without checking.

## 5. Not construction — do not use 6 feet

- **General industry (this answer):** 29 CFR 1910.28 → **4 ft (1.2 m)**.
- **Construction:** 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) → **6 ft (1.8 m)** for unprotected sides and edges; 1926 Subpart M also uses 10 ft for scaffolds and 15 ft for certain steel-erection work. These figures do **not** apply to general industry employers.
- Other OSHA parts have their own rules: shipyard employment (29 CFR 1915), longshoring (1918), and agriculture (1928). Confirm the part that covers the operation before applying 4 ft.

## 6. Definitions and measurement

- **Walking-working surface** (1910.21(b)): any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- **Unprotected sides and edges** (1910.21(b)): any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.
- **Lower level:** 1910.28 does not define the term separately. Measure vertically from the walking-working surface the employee is on down to the surface to which the employee could fall; the trigger is the fall distance the employee is actually exposed to, not the height of the building or the elevation of the floor slab.
- **Height measurement:** vertical distance from the walking-working surface to the lower level, taken at the unprotected edge. If the exposure reaches 4 ft anywhere along that edge, protection is required for the exposed employee.

## 7. State-plan states

Twenty-plus states and territories operate OSHA-approved State Plans. They must be **at least as effective** as federal OSHA and may be **more stringent** (lower trigger heights, stricter means of protection). Example: Oregon OSHA Division 2, Subdivision D mirrors the federal 4-ft trigger in 1910.28(b)(12)–(15). For a multi-state employer, verify the specific state plan's text; a state plan may not be *less* protective than 4 ft for this hazard, but it may require more.

## 8. One-line compliance statement for use in a policy or audit

> "Employees on walking-working surfaces with unprotected sides or edges 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level are protected by a guardrail system, safety net system, or personal fall protection system, per 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) and (b)(15); exposures below 4 feet are evaluated under the applicable paragraph of 1910.28(b) (e.g., dangerous equipment, openings) and under the General Duty Clause, 29 U.S.C. 654(a)(1), where a recognized hazard remains."

## 9. Traceability

- 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15), (b)(6), (b)(7), (b)(11), (b)(12), (b)(13), (b)(14) — quoted from the 2025 edition of 29 CFR Chapter XVII, Part 1910, Subpart D (govinfo PDF/XML and eCFR, fetched 2026-11-16).
- Definitions — 29 CFR 1910.21(b) / Subpart D definitions page (eCFR; Oregon OSHA Division 2 mirror).
- Construction contrast — 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) (6 ft), stated from the standard, not from the fetched excerpts.

verdict.summary:
RESERVE FUEL FOR A HELICOPTER BEGINNING A VFR FLIGHT IN THE UNITED STATES

1. DIRECT ANSWER

A helicopter must carry, beyond the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing, enough fuel to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. This is the same for day and night VFR. The governing rule is 14 CFR 91.151(b) for Part 91 operations; 14 CFR 135.209(b) imposes the identical 20-minute rotorcraft reserve for Part 135 (commercial helicopter) VFR operations.

Answer in the form requested: 20 minutes.

2. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim)

14 CFR 91.151 — Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions:

"(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

14 CFR 135.209 — VFR: Fuel supply:

"(a) No person may begin a flight operation in an airplane under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

3. APPLICABILITY — WHY THE ANSWER IS 20 MINUTES UNDER EITHER PART

- Part 91: 91.151(b) is written for "rotorcraft" and applies to any person beginning a VFR flight in the United States under the general operating rules. No day/night split.
- Part 135: 135.209(b) is written for "helicopter" and applies to VFR flight operations conducted for compensation or hire under Part 135. No day/night split.
- Because both parts specify 20 minutes for rotorcraft, the answer does not change if the flight turns out to be a for-hire operation. The 30-minute day / 45-minute night figures are airplane-only and must not be applied to a helicopter.
- Part 121: VFR helicopter operations under Part 121 are effectively nonexistent in US civil operations. If one were contemplated, the Part 121 fuel rules (121.639 VFR domestic, 121.641/121.643/121.645/121.647) would have to be checked separately; they are outside the scope of this answer and are not a realistic case for the question asked. The 20-minute figure above is the operative legal minimum for every practical US helicopter VFR operation.

4. WHAT THE 20 MINUTES IS MEASURED AGAINST — COMPLIANCE DETAIL

To be compliant, at the moment the flight begins (i.e., at takeoff), the fuel on board must satisfy all of the following simultaneously:

(a) Trip fuel: enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions along the planned route, at normal cruising speed.
(b) Reserve: an additional 20 minutes of flight at normal cruising speed, computed on the same wind/forecast basis.
(c) Usable fuel only: the reserve must be usable fuel. Unusable fuel specified in the rotorcraft flight manual (e.g., the unusable portion in each tank, or fuel that cannot be delivered in the expected attitude) does not count toward either the trip fuel or the 20-minute reserve.
(d) No alternate fuel is required for VFR. Under VFR there is no regulatory requirement to carry fuel to a destination alternate (that requirement, 14 CFR 91.167, is an IFR rule). The only regulatory add-on beyond trip fuel for a VFR helicopter is the 20-minute reserve.
(e) Taxi, hover, run-up, and air-traffic delays are not separately mandated by the rule, but they consume fuel and must be accounted for inside the pilot's own planning; they are not permitted to erode the 20-minute reserve.
(f) "Normal cruising speed" means the speed/burn the aircraft is actually expected to be operated at in cruise for that flight — not best-range or maximum-endurance speed. The reserve must be computed at that normal cruise burn.

Formula: Minimum fuel at takeoff = (trip fuel to first point of intended landing, wind-adjusted, at normal cruise) + (normal cruise fuel flow x 20/60).

5. CONVERTING THE 20 MINUTES TO A QUANTITY (if gallons or pounds are wanted)

Reserve quantity = normal cruise fuel flow / 3 (because 20 minutes = one-third of an hour).

- Gallons (avgas or Jet A): reserve gal = (cruise burn in gal/hr) / 3.
- Pounds: reserve lb = reserve gal x 6.0 lb/gal for 100LL avgas, or x 6.7 lb/gal for Jet A/Jet A-1.
- Kilograms: reserve kg = (cruise burn in kg/hr) / 3.

Illustrative worked examples (numbers are illustrative of typical cruise burns only; the operator must use the actual aircraft's flight-manual/POH cruise fuel flow):
- Piston light helicopter burning 15.0 gal/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 15.0 / 3 = 5.0 US gal (about 30 lb of 100LL).
- Piston light helicopter burning 8.4 gal/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 8.4 / 3 = 2.8 US gal (about 17 lb of 100LL).
- Turbine helicopter burning 400 lb/hr at normal cruise: reserve = 400 / 3 = 133 lb (about 20 US gal of Jet A at 6.7 lb/gal).

These quantities are the reserve only; trip fuel to the first point of intended landing is added on top.

6. COMMON ERRORS THIS ANSWER GUARDS AGAINST

- Applying the airplane 30-minute day / 45-minute night reserve to a helicopter. Wrong: rotorcraft get 20 minutes, day and night, under both 91.151(b) and 135.209(b).
- Assuming a helicopter needs a larger night reserve than a day reserve. Wrong: the rotorcraft paragraph contains no day/night distinction.
- Treating the 20 minutes as including the flight to the destination. Wrong: it is "after that" — in addition to fuel to the first point of intended landing.
- Computing the reserve at max-endurance or best-range speed to shrink it. Wrong: the rule specifies normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption.
- Counting unusable fuel toward the reserve. Wrong: the fuel must be usable.
- Assuming a VFR alternate fuel requirement exists. It does not; there is no VFR destination-alternate fuel rule for helicopters.
- Assuming a Part 135 helicopter gets a different (larger) VFR reserve. It does not under 135.209(b); however, Part 135 operators may have additional fuel requirements imposed through operations specifications and their FAA-approved fuel policy, which must be checked separately.

7. LEGAL MINIMUM VS. PRUDENT PRACTICE

The 20 minutes is a legal floor, not a target. Standard helicopter safety practice, and the guidance in FAA/industry helicopter training material, is to plan a substantially larger reserve — commonly 30 minutes or more, and more still for night, over-water, mountainous, or degraded-weather (IIMC-risk) flights — plus a personal-minimum buffer. Operator fuel policy, insurance conditions, and Part 135 operations specifications may also require more than 20 minutes. None of these change the regulatory answer: 20 minutes.

8. SOURCES CONSULTED

- 14 CFR 91.151 (eCFR, current) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151
- 14 CFR 91.151 (2026 GPO CFR XML, Title 14 vol. 2) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol2/xml/CFR-2026-title14-vol2-sec91-151.xml
- 14 CFR 135.209 (2026 GPO CFR PDF, Title 14 vol. 3) — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2026-title14-vol3/pdf/CFR-2026-title14-vol3-sec135-209.pdf
- Related Part 135 helicopter VFR sections reviewed in the same volume (135.203, 135.205, 135.207) for context on helicopter VFR operating limitations.

quotes.whole:
Abstract
This document formally deprecates Transport Layer
Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).
Accordingly, those documents have been moved
to Historic status. These versions lack support for current
and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and
various government and industry profiles of applications using
TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2
became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008
(subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing
sufficient time to transition away from older versions.
Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the
attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and
streamlines library and product maintenance.¶
This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0
(RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS
version 1.1.¶
This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or
TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best
practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195.¶
Status of This Memo
This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice.¶

Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246]
and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by
TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security
(DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2
[RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further
deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.
Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status.¶
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:¶
They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.¶
There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites, especially
authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) ciphers,
which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2. Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in the
registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447], which indicates that such entries are not
recommended by the IETF.¶
The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.¶
The authentication of the peers depends on SHA-1 signatures.¶

Acknowledgements
Authors' Addresses
1.  Introduction
Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1
[RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now
itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446].  Datagram Transport
Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS
1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012.  Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate
TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.  Accordingly, the aforementioned
documents have been moved to Historic status.
Technical reasons for deprecating these versions include:
*  They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no
longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes
TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement.
*  There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites,
especially authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD)
ciphers, which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2.  Note that
registry entries for no-longer-desirable ciphersuites remain in
the registries, but many TLS registries were updated by [RFC8447],
which indicates that such entries are not recommended by the IETF.
*  The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash.
